# Diversification Strategy — Second Consultation Draft

**Prepared for:** Board Strategy Session (Q+1) | **Owner:** [Programme Lead] | **Financial review:** CFO
**Status:** Revised following first-round critique. Recommendation now stated; arithmetic now present.

---

### How this draft differs from the first

The first version described a way of thinking and called it a strategy. The three questions where money actually gets committed — how much, build or buy, and how to stop — were missing. They are the substance of this version. The recommendation is in §0; the arithmetic that produces it is in §2; everything else supports one or the other.

All monetary figures are **placeholders using an illustrative £200m revenue base**, shown so that Finance can replace them with real numbers without redesigning the logic. Where a number is load-bearing, I have said so.

**Circulation, corrected.** The prior draft proposed showing this to customers' technical buyers. That was wrong — it is a confidentiality exposure, and if we are listed, potentially an MNPI problem. Corrected sequence: **Chair and CFO first, then flagship business lead, then Audit/Risk chair, then the full board.** Customer input comes from **NDA-bound, non-attributed discovery interviews** run by a third party, with a discussion guide that never discloses our strategic options. Nobody outside the company sees this document.

---

## §0 Recommendation

**Do this:**

1. **Reset the target in contribution terms.** Our concentration is worse than the board thinks: 95% of revenue, but roughly **98% of contribution**. Recommended seven-year target: **flagship ≤88% of contribution and ≤80% of revenue** — not the 75% revenue figure that is circulating informally, because the two are not the same ambition and the difference is roughly £30m of acquisition capital (§2).
2. **Accept that acquisition is load-bearing, not optional.** Organic build in Rings 1–3 gets us to roughly £30m of new revenue in seven years at P50. The target needs ~£54m. **The gap is bought, not built.** This is the single biggest change from the first draft.
3. **Fund a portfolio, not a project, split 70/20/10** between anti-stagnation growth (correlated, high-probability), anti-fragility options (decorrelated, venture-sized), and cheap optionality (platform, licensing, minority stakes). Two mandates, two metric sets, one envelope (§6).
4. **Cap the envelope at ≈£88m over seven years** — £28m cumulative at-risk organic spend (funded from Ring 0 pricing uplift, not reserves) and up to £60m of acquisition capital (funded from free cash flow and surplus reserves) (§3).
5. **Spend twelve weeks and ~£400k on Gate 0 before committing anything else.** Three workstreams: failure autopsy, capability audit, **and a discontinuity assessment** — the last was absent from the first draft and it is the variable that sets the size of the whole programme (§4).
6. **Pre-sign kill criteria before each tranche releases, with kill authority held by the CFO, never the sponsor** (§9).

**Conditions under which I would abandon this recommendation:** stated explicitly in §15.

---

## §1 What we are solving for

The board has named *concentration risk*. Two distinct problems are tangled inside that phrase, and they have different remedies:

| Concern | What it is | What answers it |
|---|---|---|
| **Fragility** | One shock removes most of our earnings | Earnings sources that fail in *different* scenarios; contract structure; balance-sheet strength; capital return |
| **Stagnation** | Earnings are safe but will not grow | New demand — which may or may not require new products |

An adjacency sold to the same buyer through the same channel grows earnings and does almost nothing for fragility, because it dies in the same event. Most "diversification" programmes are anti-stagnation programmes wearing the other name. We should label ours honestly and budget for both (§6).

### 1.1 The concentration is worse than stated

| | Revenue | Contribution (illustrative) | Share of contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flagship | £190m | £85.5m @ 45% | **97.7%** |
| Everything else | £10m | £2.0m @ 20% | 2.3% |
| **Total** | **£200m** | **£87.5m** | |

A mature, defended niche product carries high margin precisely because the market is slow and the investment cycle is over. Everything we add — services, managed offerings, implementation, mid-market variants — will carry **lower gross margin and higher cost-to-serve**. So revenue concentration will fall faster than contribution concentration, and the board's real concern is earnings.

Two consequences we should agree now rather than discover in year two:

- **The target must be stated in contribution terms.** Revenue diversification is the easier number and the less meaningful one.
- **The programme is margin-dilutive for approximately four years, by design.** If new lines are judged against 45% flagship contribution in year two, they will be starved — which is one of the failure modes we are trying not to repeat.

### 1.2 Three framing points I will defend

- **Harvest-and-return is a live baseline at every gate.** A profitable niche leader run for cash and capital return beats most diversification attempts on a risk-adjusted basis. Unless "do nothing new, return the capital" is genuinely available at each gate, the gates are ceremonial and every proposal passes.
- **The scarce resource is management attention and internal credibility, not cash.** Cash was why the last two attempts were possible; it was not why they were sufficient. (Amending the first draft's line: cash is not a *substitute* for a capability. In a fragmented adjacency full of undercapitalised specialists, balance-sheet strength genuinely *is* a durable advantage — that is the core of a roll-up thesis, and §8 relies on it.)
- **Two visible failures have created an internal allergy.** People will watch this expecting it to fail. That is a governance design constraint, not a morale issue, and it is why §9 and §11 are as detailed as they are.

---

## §2 The arithmetic, done

### 2.1 The scale of the task

Index the flagship at 95, everything else at 5. The flagship compounds at 2%.

| Target (Year 7) | Flagship rev | Total rev needed | New-line rev needed | Growth on today's £10m | CAGR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flagship ≤75% of **revenue** | £218m | £291m | **£73m** | 7.3× | **33%** |
| Flagship ≤80% of **revenue** | £218m | £272m | **£54m** | 5.4× | **28%** |
| Flagship ≤85% of **revenue** | £218m | £256m | **£38m** | 3.8× | **21%** |

### 2.2 The same targets in contribution — the number that matters

Assume new lines mature at **25% contribution margin** against the flagship's 45% (Finance to challenge; the conclusion is insensitive to ±5pts).

| Contribution-concentration target (Y7) | Flagship contribution | New-line contribution needed | New-line **revenue** implied | Equivalent rev

# Legacy Product End-of-Life & Migration Program

## Guiding Principles

1. **Migrate revenue, not just users.** A third of profit is at stake. Every decision — timeline, feature rebuilds, incentive spend — gets evaluated against retained ARR, not migration counts.
2. **Certainty beats generosity.** Customers defect when they're uncertain, not when they're informed. Publish firm dates and a firm feature-disposition list, then never move them. Use paid extensions as the pressure valve instead of deadline slippage.
3. **Honor the legacy product.** The most loyal customers built their operations on it. Messaging celebrates its history and sells the future; it never disparages the platform they chose.
4. **Contain risk in parallel.** Knowledge loss and security exposure get addressed from day one, independent of the customer-facing timeline.
5. **Never promise what contracts or certifications can't deliver.** No date is published until the legal contract inventory and the compliance certification audit confirm the timeline is deliverable for every obligated account.

**Program clock.** P0 = program start (internal). T0 = public EOL announcement, which occurs at P0+3, at the end of Phase 0. All milestones below are stated relative to T0. Total runway: 48 months from announcement (51 from program start).

---

## Phase 0: Fact Base (P0 to P0+3, pre-announcement)

Do not announce anything until this is complete.

- **Usage and dependency mapping.** Instrument or survey the legacy base: which niche features each account actually uses, how deeply, and how much ARR is attached to each feature.
- **Customer segmentation.** Tier the base by ARR, strategic value, feature-gap severity, regulatory exposure, and defection risk. Produce a named list of the top 15–25 accounts (likely 60–70% of legacy ARR) and flag every account that has threatened to leave.
- **Legal contract inventory (new, gating).** Catalog every installed-base agreement: multi-year terms, perpetual licenses, contractual support/maintenance obligations, auto-renewal clauses, MFN provisions, and EOL/termination rights. Flag every agreement whose support rights extend past T+48 and assign a per-account disposition: negotiate an amendment (with consideration), buy out the obligation, or — as a last resort, with legal sign-off — service it inside the sustaining tier. **Legal sign-off on the company's right to enforce the T+48 date under each contract template is a hard precondition for the announcement.**
- **Compliance certification audit (new, gating).** Inventory every certification and attestation the legacy product carries (FedRAMP, SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA BAAs, PCI DSS, data-residency commitments, industry-specific). Gap-assess the new platform against it, assign committed attainment dates to each missing certification, and fund the certification workstream from P0. Regulated customers cannot migrate without parity — their timelines are sequenced to cert dates, not to incentives.
- **Competitive exposure analysis.** For each high-risk account, document the realistic alternative vendors and their switching costs — this calibrates how much commitment each account can demand.
- **Knowledge capture.** Begin recorded architecture walkthroughs, documentation sprints, and pairing rotations with the retiring engineers *now*. Offer retention bonuses keyed to program milestones and emeritus contractor agreements post-retirement.
- **Security baseline.** Threat-model the legacy stack, pre-stage a patch pipeline that a skeleton crew can operate, and run a penetration test before the wind-down begins.

---

## Sunset Timeline & Support Policy

| Milestone | Timing | Policy |
|---|---|---|
| Public EOL announcement | T0 (= program month 3) | Full timeline, feature dispositions, compliance roadmap, and migration paths published simultaneously |
| End of new sales | T+12 | No new legacy licenses; renewals only; no new or renewed contract term may extend past T+48 (pre-existing obligations handled per the legal inventory) |
| End of standard support | T+30 | Until then: critical bug fixes + security patches. No new features after T0 |
| End of extended support | T+36 | Months 30–36: security patches only, at a 15–25% support uplift |
| Hard end of life | T+48 | Months 36–48 — the final 12 months — are the paid, named-account-only extension: "sustaining support" for named strategic accounts at ~2x pricing |
| Post-EOL data window | T+48 → T+54 | Hosted legacy environments go read-only; final 6-month export window; then certified deletion (see Data Stewardship) |
| Emergency CVE window | T+48 → T+60 | Narrowly scoped emergency patch clause (defined below) |

**Contractual guardrails:**

- Every renewal and new-business contract signed after T0 references the EOL dates explicitly; customers sign a security-risk acknowledgment for any post-EOL operation.
- Sales compensation is re-pointed at the new platform; legacy renewals pay out at a reduced rate to eliminate perverse incentives.
- **No new legacy features after T0**, with one exception class: features that *enable migration* (export tools, sync bridges).

**Post-EOL emergency patch policy (published at T0, so it is policy, not capitulation):**

- Scope: only CVEs that are (a) CVSS ≥ 9.0 or under active exploitation, and (b) remotely exploitable without authentication.
- Window: 12 months post-EOL, through T+60. Delivery is a patch or documented mitigation/isolation guidance, best-effort, no SLA, no functional fixes.
- After T+60: mitigation guidance only. All customers still running legacy at T+48 have signed the risk acknowledgment and received isolation hardening guidance.

**Pre-defined extension conditions (board-approved at T0).** Rigidity is a policy, not a blind spot. The board pre-approves the exact, sole conditions under which a one-time extension of up to 6 months would be considered:

1. Fewer than 60% of legacy ARR migrated or under signed migration commitment by T+24; **or**
2. A compliance certification blocking more than 15% of legacy ARR slips past its committed date; **or**
3. Contractual obligations identified in the legal inventory, covering more than 10% of legacy ARR, cannot be amended or bought out.

If triggered: one extension, announced once, with sustaining pricing escalating to 2.5x and no possibility of a second. Every other date in the program stays fixed.

---

## EOL Data Stewardship

- **Export guarantee.** Full data export in documented, open formats, with schema documentation, available from T0 through T+54. Export tooling is feature-frozen (but maintained) at T+36 so customers can rely on it.
- **Read-only tail.** Hosted legacy environments remain readable for 6 months post-EOL (T+48 → T+54) for final export and audit support.
- **Escrow for regulated customers.** Optional third-party escrow of data, schema documentation, and export utilities for customers with retention or audit obligations.
- **Certified deletion.** At T+54, hosted data is deleted with written attestation per account; exceptions only where legally required, documented individually.
- **On-prem/perpetual licensees.** Final export utility and schema documentation delivered by T+42; signed risk acknowledgment required to operate past T+48.

---

## Feature Disposition: Rebuild vs. Retire

Score every niche capability on five axes: ARR dependency, breadth of usage, rebuild cost, strategic fit with the new platform, and availability of substitutes (workarounds, partners, APIs). This produces four dispositions:

| Disposition | Criteria | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| **Rebuild natively** | High ARR dependency; broad usage or strategic fit | Committed publicly with target release dates; contractually committed to top accounts |
| **Partner-delivered** | Real demand, better served by ecosystem | Certified integration partner + co-marketed solution before T+18 |
| **Managed workaround** | Narrow, high-value (one or two large accounts) | Professional-services engagement or API-based bridge; priced accordingly |
| **Retire** | Low usage, low ARR | 18+ months notice, data-export tooling, and a documented transition path |

**The feature-disposition list is the single most important artifact in the program.** Publish it at T0 alongside the dates. The large customers threatening to leave are mostly reacting to uncertainty about "their" features — a public commitment with dates converts a threat into a negotiation. Maintain a per-customer **parity dashboard** ("your 9 critical capabilities: 7 available, 1 in beta Q3, 1 partner-delivered — your required attestations: SOC 2 ✓, FedRAMP in audit, expected Q2") so every account sees its own functional *and* compliance path.

**Dispute path for contested dispositions.** Customers get a 90-day window after T0 to contest any disposition with usage and business evidence. A review board (product lead, CS lead, account executive) re-scores the feature with the customer's data and decides within 30 days; the published list is updated. If "retire" stands and the customer still objects, offer a managed-workaround engagement at defined pricing or a clean contractual exit (pro-rated termination right). A clean exit is cheaper than a hostile hostage.

---

## Migration Incentives & Tooling by Tier

### Tier 1 — Strategic (top 15–25 accounts, most legacy ARR)
- Named migration team: solutions architect + dedicated engineer + executive sponsor.
- **Contractual feature commitments** with dates and service credits if missed — the antidote to defection threats.
- **Dual-run license:** operate legacy and new platform in parallel at no extra cost for up to 18 months.
- Price lock: legacy-equivalent pricing on the new platform for 2–3 years.
- Free data migration and professional services; quarterly migration steering reviews with the customer's leadership.
- For regulated Tier 1 accounts: migration plan contractually sequenced to certification attainment dates, with interim compensating controls documented.

### Tier 2 — Mid-market
- **Like-for-like cost guarantee (new):** where the new platform's pricing model differs structurally (per-seat vs. usage-based), total cost for equivalent usage is capped at legacy spend plus a small index (5–10%) for 24 months post-migration. This replaces or supplements credits where sticker shock — not the discount level — is the real churn driver.
- Migration credits (10–20% of first-year new-platform spend), with **deadline-driven step-downs** — best terms for migrating by T+18, reduced by T+30.
- **Bill-shock protection:** the migration assessment tool produces a personalized cost comparison under the customer's actual usage before they commit; first-year overage above the estimate is capped (15%) with true-up credits.
- Fixed-fee migration packages delivered with certified partners; free sandboxes, group workshops, office hours.

### Tier 3 — Long tail / SMB
- Self-serve migration wizard, in-app upgrade prompts, automated configuration conversion, and a published pricing calculator with a first-year price cap for migrators.
- Modest discount for self-migration by deadline.
- Accept that some long-tail churn is economically rational; do not spend Tier 1 dollars here. Optionally, evaluate **divestiture or a third-party maintenance handoff** for customers who will never migrate — it recovers some value and keeps them off your security exposure.

### Tooling (built program months 3–12; GA by T+9, before Tier 1 production migrations begin and before Tier 2 incentives open)
- **Migration assessment tool** that scans a customer's legacy usage and outputs their feature gaps, dispositions, compliance requirements, and a like-for-like cost comparison.
- Automated data-migration and configuration-conversion utilities with validation reports.
- **Parallel-run sync bridge** between old and new platforms, plus a tested rollback path.
- Migration runbooks, training, and a certification track for customer admins and partners.

---

## Retention Plan for Defection-Risk Accounts

**Named-account program.** Every account that has threatened to leave gets: a C-level sponsor matched to their C-level, a jointly authored migration plan, and contractual remedies (credits or opt-out windows) if committed feature dates slip. Giving customers a remedy *inside* the relationship removes their reason to leave preemptively.

**Lighthouse strategy.** Identify 2–3 referenceable strategic accounts and migrate them early at deliberately high cost. Their success stories become the sales asset that de-risks everyone else's decision.

**Risk scoring and early warning.** Score each Tier 1 account monthly on: feature-gap severity, compliance-gap status, migration milestone progress, new-platform usage, executive engagement, support-ticket sentiment, and competitive signals (RFP activity, job postings for competitor skills). Deteriorating scores trigger the escalation path within two weeks, not at renewal time.

**Save plays, in order of escalation:**
1. Re-negotiated feature commitments or delivery dates.
2. Extended dual-run or time-boxed sustaining support (within the T+48 hard stop).
3. Commercial restructuring (price protection, phased migration by business unit).
4. CEO-to-CEO engagement with a bespoke arrangement — reserved for accounts whose loss would cascade.

**Never do:** backport new-platform features to legacy to placate a holdout. It undermines the entire program's credibility.

---

## Internal Enablers

- **Engineering continuity:** retention bonuses tied to T+30 and T+48; every legacy system documented and paired by T+12; skeleton patch crew staffed and drilled before retirements begin.
- **Support-org redeployment (new):** legacy support staff receive retention bonuses through T+36, new-platform retraining and certification starting at T+6, and priority placement into migration squads and Tier 1 dedicated-engineer roles. A formal internal redeployment plan is published by T+12 — without it, pre-emptive attrition becomes a support risk in its own right.
- **Partner & reseller transition (new):** partner margins re-pointed to the new platform at parity or better; legacy resale commissions sunset at T+12 alongside end of new sales; certified partners earn migration-service revenue on Tier 2 fixed-fee packages, with certification free during the program; distributor and reseller contracts amended to reference the EOL dates.
- **Security posture:** critical-patch commitment honored through T+36 (breaking it accelerates defection); published customer guidance on isolating legacy deployments; incident-response plan staffed through T+48, with an IR retainer covering the emergency-CVE window through T+60.
- **Financial guardrails:** model incentive spend against retained ARR (target: incentives cost a fraction of one year's churned revenue); plan for 5–15% realistic legacy ARR attrition; burn down legacy infrastructure and support costs on a schedule tied to migration milestones.

---

## Governance & Metrics

- **Program office** with a dedicated leader, reporting to a steering committee of the CPO, CRO, CTO, CFO, and General Counsel; board-level visibility on legacy ARR retention quarterly.
- **KPIs:** % of legacy ARR migrated or under signed migration commitment; feature-parity coverage %; compliance-parity coverage % for regulated ARR; incentive spend per retained ARR dollar; Tier 1 health scores; legacy cost burn-down; security incidents.
- **Stage gates:** internal thresholds governing phase transitions — e.g., ≥70% of legacy ARR migrated or committed before entering the security-only phase at T+30; all compliance certifications committed for regulated ARR attained by T+24; knowledge capture complete by T+12. If a gate is missed, the first response is pushing the paid extension tier harder; only the pre-defined board conditions (above) can move a date.

We recommend a sequenced hybrid of three of the four options, plus a fourth move the menu omits:

1. **Fortify the premium position** on *provable* durability — anchored by a 10-year warranty — rather than on prestige.

# Margin-Recovery Strategy Under Sustained Cost Inflation

## 1. Situation Read

Three lessons from the last 18 months should shape the plan:

1. **Blunt increases fail because elasticity is heterogeneous.** Volume fell "faster than forecast" in price-sensitive segments — the increases were applied where they couldn't stick, and likely under-priced where they could have.
2. **The real battleground is per-unit economics, not shelf price.** Competitors' shrinkflation and tactical discounting make shelf-price comparisons noise. Win on margin per unit while *appearing* competitive on absolute price points.
3. **Retailer acceptance is negotiated, not notified.** The delisting signals that increases were presented as cost pass-throughs rather than as joint category plans.

**Objective:** recover ~6 gross-margin points **net of volume and mix effects** over 12–18 months, spread across five levers so no single lever (especially list price) carries the load.

---

## 2. Fact Base First (Days 0–60)

- **Pocket-price waterfall** per SKU × customer: list → invoice discounts → trade spend → promo allowances → slotting → freight → deductions/fines → pocket price. Expect 1–3 points of pure leakage (stale terms, unauthorized deductions, unearned allowances).
- **Decompose the 6-point loss** into input cost vs. net price vs. mix vs. trade leakage — this calibrates how much each lever must deliver.
- **Refresh elasticities at SKU × channel × segment level**, using the two failed increases as natural experiments. The old forecast model is proven wrong; do not reuse it.
- **Competitive dashboard in price per 100g/oz and per serving**, tracking competitor pack-size changes and promo depth — this cuts through the shrinkflation fog and shows whether you are actually disadvantaged or merely appear to be.
- **Cost-to-serve by customer**: order size, drop frequency, pallet efficiency, DSD vs. warehouse. Several accounts are likely unprofitable at current terms.

---

## 3. Recovery Bridge: Gross-to-Net

The bridge below is deliberately shown **gross, then net of volume/mix offsets** — price-driven recovery is partially consumed by volume deleverage (lost units worsen fixed-cost absorption) and by unit declines on resized packs. Leadership should be quoted the **net range**, never the gross.

| Lever | Gross (pts) | Volume/mix offset (pts) | Net (pts) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Net list-price recovery | 2.5–3.0 | –0.75 to –1.25 | 1.5–2.0 |
| Trade & promo efficiency | 1.25–1.75 | –0.25 to –0.50 | 0.75–1.25 |
| Pack architecture & mix | 1.25–1.75 | –0.25 to –0.50 | 0.75–1.25 |
| Cost engineering | 1.5–2.0 | ~0 (gated by equivalence testing) | 1.5–2.0 |
| Leakage recovery (deductions, stale terms) | 0.5–1.0 | 0 | 0.5–1.0 |
| **Total** | **7.0–9.5** | **–1.25 to –2.25** | **5.0–7.5** |

The plan is sized so the **net midpoint (~6.25) clears the 6-point target**, with a downside of ~5. Offset assumptions come from the refreshed elasticity work (§2), not from the legacy forecast. If tracking falls below a 5-point annualized run-rate, pre-defined contingency levers activate (§11): a second-cycle Tier A move, accelerated cost-out, and deeper tail-SKU pruning. If tracking exceeds plan, bank the surplus — do not concede it early in retailer negotiations.

---

## 4. List-Price Strategy: Surgical, Staged, Net-Focused

Segment the portfolio into three tiers using the refreshed elasticities:

- **Tier A — Price leaders** (low elasticity, strong equity, premium/impulse/single-serve): full cost pass-through, lead the market, go first.
- **Tier B — Core** (moderate elasticity): staged partial pass-through in 3–5% steps, ~2× per year, monitored against private-label and competitor gaps.
- **Tier C — Price-sensitive traffic SKUs** (high elasticity, staples, family budget items): **minimal or no list moves.** Recover margin here through pack architecture (§5) and promo redesign (§7) — this is where the volume forecast broke.

Operating rules:

- **Protect psychological price points** ($1.99, $2.49, $4.99). When economics force crossing one, change the pack rather than the sticker — the pack mechanics for this are in §5.
- **Hold price-gap corridors** vs. private label (a 15–30% premium ceiling is a common food-category pattern — treat as a *calibration starting point* and set the actual corridor from your own trade-down history). Breaching the corridor accelerates trade-down faster than any increase recovers.
- **Recover net, not just list.** Convert part of the recovery into reduced promo depth and restructured allowances (mechanics in §7) so shelf prices move less than your economics improve.
- **Pre-agree a 4–8 week "bridge"** (feature/display support) after each increase to manage the velocity dip — with a defined exit, so bridges don't become permanent spend.

---

## 5. Pack Architecture: The Workhorse Lever

Rebuild the price-pack ladder rather than shrinking silently:

- **Entry/trial packs** at iconic low price points for dollar, discounter, and convenience channels — protects price-sensitive households and keeps them in the franchise.
- **Core sizes** re-pointed so absolute shelf price stays competitive while per-unit price recovers. This is how the price-point rule (§4) is executed: cross a threshold by changing the pack, not the sticker.
- **Value/multipacks and club sizes** for heavy users — better margin per unit and a hedge against consumers exiting the category.
- **Channel-exclusive sizes/formats** so retailers cannot be directly price-matched against each other — this also defuses the "your competitor sells it cheaper" negotiation tactic.
- **Shrink vs. resize vs. reformulate:** prefer *visible-value resizing* (portion control, freshness, lunchbox formats) over silent shrinkage, which risks media/consumer backlash and retailer unit-price transparency. Cap per-unit step-ups at ~5–8% per move (calibration starting point — validate against your category's unit-price sensitivity).
- **Rationalize the tail:** cut the bottom 10–20% of SKUs by contribution. Complexity quietly eats margin (changeovers, tooling, slotting). The three delisted SKUs are candidates for re-engineering and re-entry at viable price points — not re-listing as-is.

**Change-sequencing rules (anti-stacking).** Competitors are already stacking reformulation + resize + price moves, which makes elasticity unreadable and amplifies backlash risk. Do not repeat their mistake:

1. **One change at a time per SKU.** Separate any combination of {list price, pack size, formulation} by at least one clean read window — 8–13 weeks or one full promo cycle.
2. **If economics force two changes, pair price with pack** (communicable to the trade as a single event) and hold formulation for a later window. Never stack reformulation with a resize — the consumer notices "smaller *and* different" and attributes it to bad faith.
3. **Use control cells** (matched stores or customers) wherever feasible so each change gets a clean elasticity read.
4. **Exception path:** any stacking requires CMO + CFO sign-off and a pre-agreed measurement plan.

---

## 6. Mix Management

- **Premiumize deliberately.** In inflationary food markets, premium tiers are often *more* resilient ("affordable indulgence"). Shift media, innovation, and distribution targets toward premium/functional lines.
- **Channel mix:** grow club, convenience, e-commerce, and foodservice where net realization is structurally better; allocate constrained supply accordingly.
- **Customer mix:** enforce minimum order quantities, small-order surcharges, and pickup allowances to fix unprofitable account economics rather than exiting accounts.

---

## 7. Promotion Redesign

- **Cut depth before frequency.** Move 30%-off events to 20%-off; compensate with better feature/display execution. Depth drives reference-price erosion far more than frequency. (This is the mechanism behind the "recover net, not list" rule in §4.)
- **Change mechanics:** shift from straight discounts to multi-buys, bundles, and BOGO variants — these preserve the base reference price and move more units per event.
- **Exploit loyalty/digital targeting:** deliver discounts only to price-sensitive shoppers via retailer loyalty programs and retail media networks (partially retailer-funded). This is efficient price discrimination — you stop subsidizing consumers who would have paid full price.
- **Prune ruthlessly:** typically 20–30% of promo events have negative incremental ROI. Kill them and concentrate spend in fewer, bigger, better-executed events.
- **Guard the reference price:** keep promoted volume share below ~40% in sensitive categories (calibration starting point — set the actual ceiling from your reference-price data). Above that, you've trained consumers to wait and reset retailer expectations.
- **Promo calendar as currency:** the calendar is often what retailers actually want in exchange for accepting list moves — deploy it deliberately in negotiations (§10), not reactively.

---

## 8. Targeted Cost Engineering

Cost-out must fund part of the recovery so pricing doesn't carry it all:

- **Reformulation within sensory guardrails:** ingredient substitution, spec optimization, concentration — only after consumer equivalence testing, prioritized on high-volume, low-differentiation SKUs. Never cost-engineer franchise SKUs where preference drives the brand, and observe the change-sequencing rules (§5).
- **Packaging value engineering:** lightweighting, material switches, and **case-pack/shelf-ready redesigns that also cut the retailer's handling cost** — these become give-gets in negotiation.
- **Logistics:** load-fill optimization, backhaul, fuel-surcharge indexing, order minimums, customer-pickup allowances.
- **Procurement:** hedging/forward-cover policy, index-linked supply contracts, should-cost models, alternative origins.
- **Governance:** a brand-equity gate (no saving that moves preference scores) and ring-fencing so savings aren't silently conceded in the next retailer negotiation.

---

## 9. Channel and Segment Differentiation

| Channel | Pricing/pack play | Promo play |
|---|---|---|
| **National grocery (hi-lo)** | Staged list moves; full pack ladder; JBP-wrapped | Depth cuts, multi-buys, loyalty-targeted offers |
| **Mass / EDLP** | Minimal list moves; recover via cost-to-serve and terms | Fewer, shallower events; everyday margin structure |
| **Club** | Exclusive large packs; penny-margin focus | Minimal promo; demo/sampling instead |
| **Discounters / dollar** | Dedicated entry packs at fixed price points; possibly fighter brand | None — the price point *is* the promo |
| **Convenience / gas** | Single-serve at premium per-unit pricing; take full price here | Impulse-driven; minimal discounting |
| **E-commerce** | Exclusive bundles/sizes; subscribe-and-save | Digital coupons; watch algorithmic price-matching |
| **Foodservice / B2B** | Index-linked contracts, surcharges | N/A — contractual mechanisms |

**Consumer segments:** price-sensitive households get entry packs, protected price points, and targeted digital coupons; mainstream gets modest net increases on core packs; premium/insulated segments get full pass-through plus innovation.

---

## 10. Retailer Negotiation Playbook (Avoiding Further Delistings)

**Reframe the conversation** from "price increase notification" to "joint category margin-recovery plan":

1. **Pre-wire and give lead time.** 8–12 weeks' notice, aligned to planogram resets. Present a **staged 12-month roadmap** (two or three small steps) rather than one shock — predictability is worth real money to a category manager.
2. **Bring the data pack:** commodity basket indices, PPI data, third-party scan data, and your absorption history — *"we absorbed X% of a Y% cost increase over 18 months; we're passing through only part."* Show per-unit competitive comparisons proving you remain gap-disciplined.
3. **Protect retailer economics.** Offer penny-margin-neutral structures; show how the category margin *pool* grows. Convert part of your recovery into trade-terms restructuring so their shelf price moves less.
4. **Come with give-gets:** transition funding, channel-exclusive packs, incremental display support, co-funded retail media, supply-chain savings projects (case-pack redesign, shelf-ready packaging, order minimums that cut *their* labor), and service-level commitments.
5. **Know your BATNA per SKU.** Map must-stock status, velocity, and uniqueness before every conversation. Delisting threats against strong traffic brands are usually bluff; against weak tail SKUs they're fatal — so fix or proactively exit the tail on your own terms rather than being delisted.
6. **Escalation structure:** top-to-top alignment, category-captain positioning, quarterly business reviews so increases are never a surprise.

**Repairing the delisting relationship (the most delicate negotiation in this plan).** The tactical re-entry (reformulated/repacked SKUs at viable price points) is necessary but insufficient — the buyer's trust is the real casualty. Rebuild it relationally:

- **Acknowledge the failure explicitly** and return with a category recovery plan, not a re-listing ask. Lead with what the *retailer* gets: exclusive formats, co-funded media, or a joint supply-chain project that cuts their handling cost.
- **Ask for a re-listing *trial*, not a reinstatement:** 1–2 re-engineered SKUs, defined success criteria, 90-day review. A low-risk yes is easier than a full reversal, and it reopens the shelf.
- **Offer first-mover access** to a new item or pack as the trust-rebuilding concession — it costs you little and gives the buyer a win to show internally.
- **Assign a senior sponsor** and lock a quarterly cadence so the relationship never again depends on a single transaction.

**Legal guardrails (US):** Robinson-Patman requires proportionally equal terms to competing retailers. Because this plan leans heavily on channel differentiation, tighten the compliance frame: (a) channel-exclusive packs must be genuinely exclusive at UPC level to sit outside direct comparison; (b) differentiate through functionally available non-price terms and documented cost-to-serve differences; (c) if matching a competitor's offer to a specific customer, the Section 2(b) "meeting competition" defense requires good-faith verification — document it contemporaneously; (d) maintain a written terms grid showing proportional availability of allowances. No resale price maintenance anywhere; no competitor information exchange.

---

## 11. Scenarios and Contingency Triggers

The base plan assumes staged moves land as modeled. Pre-plan the branches:

| Scenario | Early indicator / trigger | Pre-planned response |
|---|---|---|
| **Competitors don't follow Tier A increases** (hold price to gain share) | Gap vs. key competitor exceeds corridor for 4 consecutive weeks; velocity declines >1.5× model | Pause the next step on affected SKUs; shift recovery to promo-depth and pack levers; deploy targeted loyalty offers. **Do not roll back list** — rollback resets credibility and is nearly impossible to re-take |
| **Competitor "honest sizing / no shrink" campaign** | Campaign launch; social-listening spike; retailer inquiries | Activate transparency narrative: visible-value formats, per-serving clarity; accelerate entry price-point packs;

# Diversification Strategy: Adjacency-Led Growth from a Strong Core

## Governing Diagnosis

The two failed attempts share a signature: they were *market-led* rather than *capability-led* — the company chased attractive markets where it had no transferable advantage. Research on adjacency moves (Zook's *Beyond the Core*; Porter's diversification tests) is consistent: diversification success rates fall sharply with "distance" from the core, and the most profitable growth comes from expanding outward from a strong core along shared capabilities, customers, or channels.

The governing principle: **diversify only where existing assets confer a genuine right to win, stage capital so every bet is affordable to lose, and never let the program threaten the cash engine that funds it.**

The company's position is favorable: profitability, cash reserves, loyal customers, and deep niche expertise mean it can be patient. The risk is not desperation — it is overpaying for growth or repeating capability drift.

---

## Step 0: Test the Baseline — Is Diversification Even the Right Move?

Before designing the program, the board should test it against the realistic alternatives, because every dollar committed must beat them:

- **Option A — Accept concentration and return reserves** (dividends/buybacks). This maximizes near-term shareholder cash but leaves the 95% dependency untouched; it pays shareholders to *hold* the risk rather than reducing it. Concentrated, mature companies also tend to trade at a valuation discount, so concentration is quietly taxing the share price.
- **Option B — Sell the company at peak.** Correct *if* the board has evidence the flagship faces disruption within a horizon where a buyer could still be convinced otherwise. Absent that evidence, selling forfeits the option value embedded in the capability base and customer franchise.
- **Option C — Capability-led diversification.** Positive expected value *only if* the company's assets confer a real right to win somewhere beyond the core — which Steps 1–3 exist to verify, not assume.

**Recommendation: Option C, with Option A as the standing benchmark.** Any venture or acquisition that cannot credibly beat returning its capital to shareholders should not be funded. This framing preempts the toughest board question and disciplines the whole program: the default use of cash is to give it back, so every diversification dollar must earn its place.

---

## Step 1: Audit the Actual Advantage Stack

Before evaluating any market, inventory what the company is genuinely better at than competitors. Sort capabilities into five buckets:

| Bucket | Examples to inventory |
|---|---|
| **Customer assets** | Brand trust, installed base, switching costs, customer data, relationships |
| **Technology/product** | Proprietary IP, manufacturing processes, engineering know-how |
| **Channel** | Sales force, distribution network, service infrastructure |
| **Operations** | Supply chain, quality systems, regulatory compliance expertise |
| **Intangibles** | Domain reputation, certifications, specialist talent |

Two disciplines make this audit useful rather than ceremonial:

1. **Differentiate, don't just list.** A capability only matters if it would make the company *better than the incumbents in the target space*. "We have good engineers" is not an advantage; "our reliability engineering exceeds anything in the adjacent category" is.
2. **Run a formal post-mortem on the two failures.** Codify specifically what "too far from our capabilities" meant — a channel we didn't understand? A technology we couldn't support? A customer with different buying behavior? Convert the findings into *hard exclusion criteria* in the evaluation screen (Step 3). Past failures are only wasted if they don't tighten the filter.

---

## Step 2: Pursue Adjacencies by Distance, Nearest First

Rank opportunities by how many of three things they share with the core: **customers, capabilities, channels.** Require at least two of three.

**Tier 1 — Customer adjacencies (lowest risk, start here).** Sell new things to the loyal base that already trusts the brand:
- Complementary products, consumables, accessories, upgrades
- Services wrapped around the flagship: maintenance, training, extended warranties, subscription/recurring-revenue layers
- These leverage brand and channel directly, require modest capital, and generate cash that funds further moves. A services layer also has a *different demand driver* than product sales (installed-base usage vs. new purchases), which genuinely reduces correlation.
- **Financing caveat:** customer financing appears on many such lists — treat it as *partner-delivered only* (a white-label arrangement with a bank or captive-finance specialist). Credit underwriting, balance-sheet risk, and lending regulation sit outside this company's capability envelope; building them in-house would repeat the original failure pattern inside the "safe" tier.
- **Two Tier 1 cautions:** (i) *Channel conflict* — selling complements or services direct can alienate the distributors the flagship depends on; decide channel architecture deliberately, e.g., route services through existing partners with revenue share. (ii) *Cannibalization* — a superb maintenance service extends product life and can slow replacement demand. That trade is usually still worth making (better you capture the service margin than a third party), but the mix math in Step 6 counts only *net additive* revenue, so model the portfolio effect honestly.

**Tier 2 — Product/technology adjacencies.** Apply core technology and manufacturing competence to adjacent product categories or use cases — ideally ones purchased by customers you already understand.

**Tier 3 — Value-chain adjacencies.** Move downstream (distribution, services, data/analytics on product usage) or selectively upstream (critical components) where it captures margin or locks in supply.

**Tier 4 — Channel/geographic adjacencies.** Be precise about what this tier does: selling the *same product* into new geographies or channels reduces *market* concentration but leaves *product* concentration — the board's stated concern — unchanged. If the flagship is disrupted, geographic spread won't save it. Treat Tier 4 as a complement that funds the program and broadens customer learning, not as progress toward the de-concentration target. And since the core market is mature globally, map it but don't count on it for growth.

**Explicitly avoid:** conglomerate-style moves into high-growth markets where the company brings no transferable advantage. That is precisely the pattern that failed twice. Growth rate of the target market is not a substitute for a right to win.

**One honest caveat:** adjacency-led diversification reduces *product-specific* risk (obsolescence, disruption of the flagship) more than *market-cycle* risk, because adjacencies share customers and demand drivers. Within the capability envelope, prioritize adjacencies with partially uncorrelated demand — services, consumables, different end-markets.

---

## Step 3: The Evaluation Screen

Every candidate must pass three sequential gates:

**Gate 1 — Strategic fit (pass/fail, using the post-mortem exclusion criteria):**
- Does at least one core capability transfer in a way that makes us *better than the incumbents there*? Force a one-page "right to win" statement. If it can't be written convincingly, stop.
- Does it share ≥2 of customers / capabilities / channels?

**Gate 2 — Porter's three tests:**
1. **Attractiveness:** Is the industry structurally profitable (not just growing)?
2. **Cost of entry:** Will entry costs (or acquisition premium) consume the likely returns?
3. **Better-off test:** Does our ownership create value the business couldn't create alone? Operationalize this with the reverse question: *"If this were a standalone venture, would we fund it — and does our ownership make it more likely to win?"* Require mechanisms (specific asset transfers: channel access, brand endorsement, manufacturing cost advantage), not adjectives ("synergies").

**Gate 3 — Portfolio and financial fit:**
- Correlation of demand drivers with the core (lower is better)
- **Net-additivity test:** how much revenue is genuinely new versus cannibalized from the flagship or pulled from partners
- Capital intensity, margin structure, path to profitability within a defined window
- Management bandwidth consumed — the hidden cost that most often damages the core

---

## Step 4: Build, Buy, or Partner

Decide based on the size of the capability gap and the urgency of the window:

| Condition | Route |
|---|---|
| Small capability gap, moderate time pressure, leverages existing assets | **Build** — cheapest, best cultural fit, slowest. Default for Tier 1 customer adjacencies. |
| Need a capability or market access you lack; demand unproven; want to limit downside | **Partner** — alliances, licensing, distribution agreements, JVs. Ideal as a low-cost probe, as *live diligence* on a potential acquisition target, and for capabilities you should never own (e.g., the financing example above). |
| Closing window, proven product-market fit, large but *integratable* capability gap | **Buy** — but disciplined: small bolt-ons adjacent to the core, not transformational deals. Integration plan and talent-retention plan *before* signing. Walk-away price set in advance. |

A powerful sequence for anything beyond Tier 1: **partner → minority stake → full acquisition.** Each step buys information and reduces uncertainty before irreversible capital is committed. Given the failure history, avoid large acquisitions in the first 2–3 years; the organization needs to rebuild its diversification muscle on smaller, winnable bets first.

---

## Step 5: Stage Investment — Two Envelopes, Both Hard-Capped

Structure the program like a venture portfolio, using discovery-driven planning — and resolve up front how organic spending and acquisition spending relate, because the growth math (Step 6) can't be met by organic investment alone.

**Envelope A — Organic ventures (annual operating budget).** Cap at 5–10% of annual operating cash flow, funded from cash, never from debt secured against the core. This is the *learning* budget: it buys information and builds the organic engine. Be honest about its scale — it funds probes and can scale one or two winners, but it cannot manufacture a 39% CAGR in non-core revenue. Its job is proof, not pace.

**Envelope B — M&A (board-approved, drawn from reserves, governed separately).** Set two hard limits: a single-deal cap (sized so no one failure can wound the balance sheet) and a cumulative program cap (e.g., a defined share of current reserves over five years, preserving a fortress balance sheet throughout). Critically, **Envelope B stays locked until Envelope A produces evidence**: acquisitions are permitted only into spaces where probes have demonstrated demand and the company's right to win. This is how the growth math gets funded without opening the door to the transformational-deal risk that destroyed the earlier attempts.

**The board's real choice is pace versus exposure.** Envelope A alone realistically delivers roughly an 85/15 mix by year five. Adding disciplined bolt-ons from Envelope B in validated spaces gets to ~75–80%. Going faster requires bigger deals — the historical failure mode at larger scale. Present this trade-off explicitly rather than hiding it inside an aspirational target.

**Ring-fence the new ventures.** Create a New Ventures unit with its own governance (a venture board), dedicated leadership, and separate P&L — but with *metered access* to core assets (brand, channel, customer data). That access is the entire rationale for related diversification; isolation would forfeit it, and absorption into the core would smother it.

**Tranche-based funding tied to proof points, not time:**

| Tranche | Purpose | Released on evidence of |
|---|---|---|
| Seed (small) | Customer discovery, prototype, assumption testing | Validated customer problem; willingness-to-pay evidence |
| Pilot (moderate) | Limited launch, real transactions | Traction, retention/repeat rates, early unit economics |
| Scale (material) | Full launch, capacity; unlocks Envelope B for this space | Proven unit economics and a credible path to target margins |

**Pre-committed kill criteria.** Define abandonment triggers *before* each tranche is released (e.g., "kill if repeat purchase < X% after 12 months of pilot"). This prevents escalation of commitment — the sunk-cost dynamic that turns small failures into expensive ones. Failure of an individual bet is expected and acceptable; *unbounded* failure is not.

**Protect the core explicitly:**
- Core leadership's incentives stay tied to the core; ventures get dedicated teams with milestone-based incentives.
- Use sub-brands or endorsed brands for riskier ventures so a visible failure cannot contaminate flagship brand equity.
- Expect a portfolio outcome: of 4–5 bets, plan for 1–2 to become material. Size each so its loss is a rounding error, not a trauma.

---

## Step 6: Sequencing and Realistic Targets

**Phase 0 (months 0–6):** Baseline test (Step 0), capability audit, failure post-mortem, adjacency map, venture governance and both envelopes stood up.
**Phase 1 (months 6–18):** Launch 2–3 Tier 1 probes from Envelope A (services layer, complementary products to existing customers). Lowest cost, fastest learning.
**Phase 2 (months 18–36):** Scale the winners, kill the losers, initiate one Tier 2 adjacency; Envelope B unlocks for the first bolt-on acquisition in a *validated* space.
**Phase 3 (years 3–5):** Second engine becomes material.

**Set targets with arithmetic, not aspiration.** If the core is 95% of revenue and grows 2%/year, then in five years the core is ~105 (indexed). To reach even an 80/20 mix, the non-core must grow from 5 to ~26 — roughly a 39% CAGR. To reach 70/30 requires ~55% CAGR. Implications:

1. Reducing concentration by *shrinking* the core is not a strategy — the mix only moves if new revenue is genuinely additive (which is why Gate 3's net-additivity test matters).
2. Envelope A alone cannot deliver that pace; reaching ~75–80% requires Envelope B bolt-ons in validated spaces by Phase 2–3.
3. A realistic five-year goal is **~75–80% flagship dependency with maintained margins**, on the way to ~65–70% by year seven. Present this to the board explicitly — vague "diversification" targets breed impatience and bad deals.

---

## Illustrative Thread (How the System Runs End to End)

*Assume, for illustration, the flagship is an industrial air compressor line sold to manufacturing plants.*

- **Audit** finds: a trusted brand among plant engineers, a 10,000-unit installed base, proprietary compressor design, a national service network, and deep reliability engineering. The failure post-mortem yields exclusion criteria: no consumer channels, no markets where buying is price-auction rather than relationship-based.
- **Tier 1 probe:** a predictive-maintenance subscription — sensors on the installed base, failure alerts, priority service — sold to existing customers through the existing service network. The IoT cloud platform is **partnered** (capability we should never own); the service itself is **built** (small gap, uses our channel). Seed: ~$1.5M from Envelope A. # Post-Merger Integration Plan: People & Organization

A note before the plan itself: the three symptoms — poaching, slow decisions, stalled synergies — look like separate problems. They aren't. They're one problem: six months in, nobody has decided what the combined company actually *is*. Talent leaves through ambiguity, decisions stall in it, and synergies hide behind it. So the real deliverable of this plan is not a document — it's **decision speed, restored in a way that preserves trust**. Everything below is sequenced to achieve that, and this time the plan follows its own logic: decide, select, retain, then standardize — in that order, with no exceptions buried in the details.

**Stated assumption:** this plan assumes the combined entity operates primarily in at-will employment jurisdictions. Where works councils or statutory consultation apply, Section 3.5's consultation track governs, and local timelines adjust without compromising the global sequence.

---

## 1. Guiding Principles

1. **Decide fast, select fair.** Speed and fairness are not in tension; slowness is what feels unfair.
2. **Individuals hear first, privately, from someone they trust.** No one learns about their own role in a town hall — and no one loses face in the process.
3. **No permanent two-in-a-box.** Co-leadership only as a time-boxed transition (≤90 days) with a single named accountable owner.
4. **Protect the magic, standardize the plumbing.** The acquired firm's agility is part of what was paid for. The instinct to standardize everything is worth resisting — politely, but firmly.
5. **One rulebook where it matters; local freedom where it doesn't.** Ambiguity about *which* applies is the current tax on every decision.
6. **Harmony is built, not declared.** The two legacy cultures will integrate through shared work, honored legacies, and fair process — not through posters.

---

## 2. Target Operating Model

**Recommendation: an integrative "best-of-both" model with two deliberate speeds.**

A holding model can't deliver the synergy case; full absorption will trigger the talent exodus that destroys the deal's logic. So:

- **Backbone (standardized):** Finance, HR operations, Legal/Compliance, IT infrastructure/security, Procurement, Quality/Regulatory — consolidated onto single platforms and one policy set. This is where the synergies live.
- **Edge (protected):** Product development, innovation teams, and customer-facing units from the founder-led firm keep their lightweight operating style — small autonomous teams, short cycles, minimal approval layers. Where their practices demonstrably outperform, they become the *combined* company's standard, not merely a preserved enclave.
- **Structure:** The fewest layers that still give clear accountability — likely delayering the hierarchical legacy org by one level, which serves the synergy case and signals that the future company is not simply the acquirer, enlarged.

**Decision rights — the single most urgent artifact.** Published within two weeks:
- A one-page charter mapping the **top 20 recurring decisions** (pricing, hiring, capex, product roadmap, vendor selection…) to a single owner each.
- **Ownership and sign-off:** the IMO drafts the charter; the **CEO signs it**; the joint steering committee ratifies it; the IMO acts as custodian and reviews it monthly. A charter without a named signer is a suggestion.
- Escalation path with a **48–72 hour SLA** — escalation is a service, not a failure.
- **Interim default rule:** until a process is formally harmonized, the legacy process of the unit doing the work governs. This one sentence restores decision speed overnight, because it eliminates "whose process applies?" as a reason to wait.

---

## 3. Leadership Selection & Resolving Duplicate Roles

**Clean-sheet approach: design the structure → define the roles → select the people. In that order.**

### 3.1 Selection criteria — published in advance

- Capability for the *future* role (not legacy title): **45%**
- Track record of delivery: **25%**
- Potential and adaptability: **20%**
- Culture-*add* behaviors (per Section 8's operating principles): **10%**

Flight risk and retention criticality are **deliberately excluded** from selection criteria. Selection picks the best leader; retention risk is managed with the retention levers in Section 4. Conflating the two rewards people for being recruitable and corrupts both decisions. Where a selection outcome would create a genuine retention emergency, the answer is a meaningful alternative role or scope — handled through Section 4 — not a distorted selection.

### 3.2 Process

- **Joint calibrated panels** — members from both legacy firms, plus an external assessor for L1/L2 roles to keep the process honest and be *seen* to be honest.
- **Open application** for key roles across both companies. Merit-based competition is the strongest signal that this isn't a takeover dressed as a merger.
- **Pre-alignment before decisions:** panel outcomes are quietly socialized with the CEO and key stakeholders before ratification, so group decisions land smoothly and without public surprise.
- **Timeline: L1 named by day 30, L2 by day 60, L3 by day 90.** The roadmap in Section 7 is built around these dates — they are the same commitment, stated once. Every week beyond day 90 is a recruiting window for competitors.

### 3.3 Interim stewardship during the selection window

The 8–13 week selection window is where duplicate incumbents are most vulnerable to poaching and most tempted to wage quiet campaigns. Rules, applied uniformly:

- **One named interim steward per function**, appointed in week 2, holds operational authority through the window. Selection as interim steward is explicitly communicated — privately and in writing — as *not* a predictor of final selection, to manage expectations in both directions.
- **The other incumbent receives a defined, dignified transition role** — leading an integration workstream, owning customer continuity for top accounts, or a scoped special project reporting to the CEO. A real mandate, not a waiting room. This preserves status, keeps their network warm for the company, and keeps them visible to the panel.
- Both conversations happen **privately, before any public signal**, ideally by a senior leader each incumbent already trusts.
- Hard stop: no interim arrangement survives past day 90.

### 3.4 Fairness safeguards

- Track selection ratios by legacy company monthly. If a skew emerges, investigate for bias — don't impose quotas, but don't ignore the data either.
- A quiet question worth asking the selection committee early: *if every top role goes to one legacy firm, what exactly did we buy?*

### 3.5 Jurisdictions and consultation

- Where works councils or statutory consultation apply: **initiate consultation in Phase 0, in parallel with design work** — not after decisions are drafted. Selection in those entities runs on a consultation track (typically adding 4–12 weeks locally), with interim stewardship extended accordingly.
- Nothing is announced in a consultation jurisdiction before obligations are met there. A compliance failure here would cost far more than the weeks it saves — in money, in legal standing, and in the trust of precisely the workforce we most need to keep.

### 3.6 For those not selected

Early, honest, private conversations; fair severance; real outplacement; alumni-grade treatment. Where possible, a graceful transition narrative agreed with the individual — people should leave with dignity intact and speak well of how they were treated. The slow bleed — keeping displaced leaders in limbo — is the most expensive option in every currency: money, morale, and reputation.

---

## 4. Critical Talent Retention

**Week 1–2: build the map.** Plot the top 75–100 people on criticality × flight risk. Include culture carriers, customer-relationship holders, and irreplaceable technical knowledge — not just top performers. Assume the founder-led firm's list is underweighted today; they usually are.

**Levers, in order of actual effectiveness for founder-led talent:**
1. **Autonomy and scope** — real decision rights, visibly granted. This group rarely stays for money alone; they stay for room to build.
2. **The founder's visible commitment** — see below; this is a scheduled action, not an open question.
3. **Stay awards** — structured as described below.
4. **Stay interviews** with a senior leader from *either* firm within two weeks; weekly flight-risk review; retention KPIs owned by named managers.

**Stay award architecture — sequenced to survive selection:**
- **Integration Retention Awards (weeks 3–6, top ~25–30):** service-based awards tied to continued employment with the *combined company* through defined milestones — **explicitly not guarantees of any specific role**, and payable even if the holder is not selected for their current role. This removes the contradiction of signing role-linked packages before selection concludes, while moving fast enough to matter.
- **Role-confirmation awards (immediately following each selection wave):** milestone-based awards (12–18 months, meaningful percentages of base) for critical people confirmed in roles, and for critical people accepting redesigned roles.
- Award letters reviewed against selection criteria to ensure no implied role promise the process cannot honor.

**Counter-offer policy (pre-agreed, so we never improvise under pressure):**
- Our posture is **preemptive**: stay interviews and early awards exist so counter-offers are rare.
- When an external offer surfaces: **48-hour response SLA**. For the top ~25, the functional leader plus CHRO hold pre-approved authority to respond within a defined band (cash, scope, title, development). Beyond the band, CEO approval — same 48 hours.
- We compete first on scope, autonomy, and growth; we match cash selectively, not reflexively. Open-ended matching teaches the organization that outside offers are the compensation review process.

**Founder engagement — a Phase 0 commitment, not a rhetorical question:**
- The deal sponsor (or the board member holding the relationship) opens the conversation **by day 10**; target **agreement in principle by day 30** on a meaningful ongoing role — innovation charter, board seat, earn-out alignment — shaped around what the founder genuinely wants their next chapter to be.
- Their loyalists are watching the founder, not the acquirer's CEO. This conversation is the single highest-leverage retention act available to us, and it belongs on the critical path with an owner and a date.

The blunt truth remains: the strongest retention lever is resolving the org chart. Poachers sell certainty; the only counter is to offer it first.

---

## 5. Processes: Standardize, Harmonize, or Leave Alone

| Standardize now (backbone) | Best-of-both (choose by evidence) | Leave alone (12+ months) |
|---|---|---|
| Financial reporting & controls | Product development cadence | Team-level rituals & norms |
| Compliance, risk, legal | Go-to-market & sales motion | Innovation workflow |
| Payroll operations | Customer success practices | Internal communication styles |
| Procurement & vendor base | Hiring bar elements | Experimentation methods |
| IT security & infrastructure | | |

**Benefits are handled separately — and deliberately not "standardized now."** Benefits takeaways during an active poaching war are self-inflicted attrition. Governing principle: **no net takeaway during integration.**
- Months 0–6: both legacy benefit structures grandfathered; payroll operations consolidated for efficiency with zero change to employee-visible value.
- Months 6–9: design harmonization toward the **richer standard** where differences are material; cost it honestly within the synergy model.
- Months 9–12: implement, only after retention packages are locked and selection is complete. Flagged as a named risk in Section 11.

**Two mechanisms make the table stick:**
- **A process registry** — one living document stating which process applies where, who owns it, and when it changes. Published in week 2. Kills the ambiguity currently taxing every decision.
- **Evidence over legacy** for the middle column: pick per process based on outcomes (cycle time, win rate, NPS), not on which firm it came from — and **pilot the chosen process in one unit before broad rollout**. Every time the acquired firm's way wins, that's a retention signal money can't buy.

---

## 6. Delivering the 15% Overhead Synergy

**The denominator, stated once and precisely:** the commitment is **15% of the combined addressable overhead base (AOB)** — combined SG&A excluding customer-facing revenue capacity and regulatory-mandated roles — measured as **exit run-rate gross savings by month 12–15**. In-year P&L impact will be lower due to timing and is reported separately; the board anchors on run-rate. **Cost-to-achieve is tracked separately** (Section 6.3), with net payback targeted at ~12 months.

**Ownership:** the **CFO owns the number** — not the IMO, not the initiative owners. Initiative owners own levers; the IMO tracks and reports; the CFO answers for the total.

### 6.1 Re-baseline and the shortfall decision tree

Re-baseline bottom-up **by day 45** — top-down salami-slicing is how synergies get announced and never land. If the re-baseline lands below 15%, the steering committee chooses, **with the board, at the re-baseline review — not later, not quietly:**

1. **Bridge:** expand scope or add levers (preferred; the gap is usually findable in procurement, footprint, and layers).
2. **Extend:** hold 15% but move full run-rate out, with board agreement.
3. **Revise:** adjust external guidance **once**, transparently, with a credible plan.

Pre-agreeing this decision tree with the board at day 45 prevents the worst outcome: a shortfall discovered late and communicated in drips.

### 6.2 The six lost months

Address them once, candidly, at the re-baseline: what was assumed, what has actually happened, the corrected trajectory with dated milestones. Then consistent quarterly reporting thereafter. One honest reset preserves credibility; a series of small surprises destroys it.

### 6.3 Lever decomposition and cost-to-achieve

| Lever | Share of target | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Org delayering & duplicate role elimination | 40–50% | Months 3–9 |
| Procurement & vendor consolidation | 15–20% | Months 4–12 |
| Facilities & real estate footprint | 10–15% | Months 6–15 |
| Systems, licenses, IT rationalization | ~10% | Months 6–15 |
| Shared services & automation | Remainder | Months 9–18 |

**Cost-to-achieve envelope (indicative, sized precisely at re-baseline; S = annual run-rate savings):**

| Category | Share of one-time budget |
|---|---|
| Severance & transition | 30–35% |
| Retention pool (both award types) | 15–20% |
| Systems migration & IT | 25–30% |
| Facilities exit costs | 10–15% |
| IMO staffing & external support | 5–10% |
| Contingency | ~10% |

Total one-time cost: **~0.8–1.0× S**, phased across months 2–15, approved by the board as a single envelope at re-baseline. Ring-fence customer-facing capacity throughout — a synergy program that dents revenue is a bad trade. Monthly run-rate tracking against plan, reported alongside financials so it cannot quietly drift.

---

## 7. Sequence & Roadmap

| Phase | Window | Key moves |
|---|---|---|
| **0 — Stabilize** | Weeks 0–2 | Interim decision-rights rule; process registry; interim stewards named (privately first); retention map + stay interviews begin; IMO stood up with real authority; founder conversation opened (day 10); consultation initiated where required; decision-cycle baseline measured |
| **1 — Design** | Weeks 2–8 | Clean-sheet TOM; synergy re-baseline (day 45) with board decision tree; **L1 selection (day 30)**; Integration Retention Awards signed (weeks 3–6); culture diagnostic; communication cadence launched |
