# Strategic Response to Low-Cost Disruption: A Conditional Dual-Track Strategy

## 1. Diagnosis: Decompose the 40% Gap Before Choosing a Weapon

The right strategy depends on what the price gap is actually made of. Three components, each with different strategic implications:

- **Channel economics (likely 25–35 points of the gap).** Appliance retail carries 25–35% margin; an online-only entrant avoids most of it. This portion is structural — it cannot be closed without channel conflict, and we should not try.
- **Product content (likely 10–20 points).** Fewer features, cheaper components, less durability engineering. This portion *is* closable through clean-sheet value engineering.
- **Overhead and margin structure (unknown).** The entrant may be genuinely lean or burning investor cash. Worth determining, but dangerous to build a strategy on either assumption.

Two facts anchor everything that follows. First, **healthy margins with six quarters of volume decline is the most dangerous position in business**: operating leverage works in reverse, and margin erosion typically lags volume erosion by 12–24 months. The P&L says we have time; the volume trend says we don't. Second, the market is **segmenting, not uniformly trading down**. The disruptor is winning "good enough" buyers — first-time purchasers, price-driven replacers, landlords, builders — while a durable "buy-it-for-life" segment remains.

**This is why the recommendation below is explicitly conditional.** The size and growth rate of the value segment is the single variable that determines the right strategy, and we do not know it today. The board should approve a *direction and a decision process*, not an irreversible commitment: a 120-day validation phase with a hard go/no-go gate and pre-committed pivot options (Section 3). That is not hedging — it is sequencing commitment behind evidence.

## 2. Options, Seriously Evaluated

| Option | Segment coverage | Cost feasibility | Speed | Culture fit | Key risk | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. Defend premium only | Shrinks over time | N/A | Fast | High | Cedes entry price point; niche retreat | Rejected as standalone; strengthened as Track 1 |
| B. Match price on core brand | Full | Impossible without gutting P&L | — | Destroys it | Brand and margin destruction | Rejected |
| C. Fighter brand | Full | Feasible only with clean-sheet cost model | 12–18 mo | Manageable with separation | Cannibalization, execution | **Recommended (conditional)** |
| D. Service/subscription (AaaS) as primary | Narrow (B2B) | Untested unit economics | Slow | Neutral | Consumer adoption unproven | Flank pilot, not primary |
| E. Acquire the disruptor | Full | Buys capability instantly | Fast | Poor — culture clash | Overpaying for burn rate | Contingent trigger |
| F. Private-label manufacturing | Value tier via retailers | Feasible | Fast | Low | Cedes consumer relationship | Utilization bridge only |

**On Option A, honestly assessed.** The ultra-premium retreat works — Miele and Sub-Zero prove it — but under specific conditions: a category with super-premium price headroom and a brand with luxury equity, not merely durability equity. Ours is a "durable premium" brand, not a luxury one, and mainline appliances have limited headroom above current price points. The deeper problem is structural: defending premium only cedes the *entry price point*, and the entry purchase is where 30-year brand relationships begin. Losing first-time buyers today means losing the premium customer pipeline of 2030. **However** — if Phase 1 research shows the value segment is small and static, this verdict flips, and Option A plus aggressive cost restructuring becomes the right answer. That is exactly what Gate 1 tests.

**On Option D.** Appliance-as-a-service fits the landlord/builder/property-management segment naturally, and our durability is an *asset* in a service model — long-life products are what an annuity business wants. But consumer subscription adoption is unproven, so it runs as a B2B pilot in Phase 2, not as the strategic core.

**On Option E.** Acquiring the disruptor buys the online capability we lack and removes the threat — but at the risk of overpaying for a cash-burning model and importing a culture clash. Hold as a live trigger: if their growth stalls and valuation resets, or if our organic build is clearly lagging at month 12, M&A moves to the front of the queue.

## 3. Recommended Strategy: Dual-Track Barbell, Conditionally Committed

**Track 1 — Sharpen the premium core. Track 2 — Launch a clean-sheet fighter brand. Enabler — A structural cost program that funds both.**

**Gate 1 (day 120–150) go/no-go criteria, agreed with the board in advance:**

- **Proceed with the fighter brand** if: (a) the value segment is ≥25% of category volume and growing; (b) gap decomposition shows at least half the gap is closable through product content and our own overhead — i.e., we can hit target cost without the retail margin; (c) willingness-to-pay research supports at least price parity with a service-backed tiebreaker.
- **Pivot A — Premium fortress:** if the value segment is small or static, drop the fighter brand, combine Option A with the full cost program, and defend the premium pipeline through targeted entry price points.
- **Pivot B — Acquire or partner:** if the gap proves mostly structural (channel economics we cannot replicate) or the capability assessment concludes we cannot build DTC competence, shift the fighter budget to acquisition of the disruptor or a value-tier manufacturer.

## 4. Track 1: Make Premium Provable and Monetizable

- **Publish reliability data** and build total-cost-of-ownership tools for consumers and retail salespeople.
- **Lead on repairability and sustainability** — longevity is an anti-landfill story aligned with right-to-repair momentum, and it gives engineers a mission worth rallying around.
- **Targeted warranty extension — costed, not free.** Extend to 10 years *only on components where field failure data supports it* (sealed systems, motors), not blanket coverage. Require actuarial sign-off; illustrative incremental reserve of 75–150 bps of premium-line revenue, carried as a marketing line item with measured conversion lift. Claim-rate tripwires: if actual claims exceed assumptions for two consecutive quarters, the extension is re-scoped before it becomes an unfunded liability. The warranty is a bet on our own reliability data — if engineering won't sign the actuarial model, marketing doesn't get to make the promise.
- **Innovate where the disruptor structurally cannot follow**: service network, installation, smart integration, trade-in and certified-refurbished programs.

## 5. Track 2: Fighter Brand — Design Principles and Pricing Logic

**Design principles** (unchanged in substance, because they are where most fighter brands die):

1. **Clean-sheet design to a target cost**, not decontenting. A premium architecture minus features is still too expensive. Target BOM at 50–60% of premium; 3–5 SKUs per category; standardized components; packaging engineered for e-commerce logistics.
2. **Separate team, separate P&L, startup mandate** — 30–50 people, 18-month clock, organizational distance from the mothership. Share the back end (manufacturing scale, supplier leverage, parts bin, service network — a decisive advantage over the disruptor); never the front end.
3. **Hard guardrails**: no shared model numbers, maintained price ladder, warranty differentiation (2-year vs. 10-year), capped feature overlap.
4. **Build vs. buy decided at Gate 1** based on the cost-gap and capability analysis.

**Pricing — resolving the tension in the original proposal.** Our own diagnosis says value buyers won't pay for extras; pricing the fighter at a blanket +5–10% "justified by service" contradicts that. Corrected logic:

- **Default to price parity** with the disruptor. At equal price, our service network, parts availability, and reliability become the *tiebreaker*, not a premium to be justified. Parity is achievable precisely because the fighter carries no retail margin on its online volume.
- **Test a +5–10% tier only where willingness-to-pay research supports it** — the landlord/builder sub-segment plausibly pays for service-backed uptime even when first-time buyers won't. Phase 1 WTP research sets the final ladder; parity is the fallback, not the stretch case.
- **Maintain the ladder**: premium at +60–80% over fighter, enforced by feature and warranty differentiation.

**Cannibalization — reconciled numbers.** Planning assumption: 10–20% of fighter volume substitutes for our own premium line (measured via switching analysis in the pilot, not guesswork). Gates: **<25% → scale; 25–35% → adjust the price ladder and feature guardrails before scaling; >35% sustained → stop.** Self-cannibalization at some margin beats losing 100% of the sale — but only within a monitored envelope.

## 6. Financial Architecture: Funding the Fight

A mid-sized manufacturer cannot fund a fighter launch, a restructuring, warranty reserves, and a retail program simultaneously out of hope. Illustrative envelope, scaled to revenue (assume $500M–1B revenue base; board substitutes actuals):

| Element | Size | Timing | Funding source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost program | 8–12% of addressable COGS over 24 months (SKU rationalization 3–5 pts, design-to-value 3–5, footprint 2–4) | Launches month 0; releases cash from month 9 | Self-funding after one-time restructuring costs |
| Fighter brand | 2–4% of revenue across 24 months (team, clean-sheet design, tooling/CM, digital build, launch marketing) | Deliberately back-loaded to months 9–24 | Released by cost program |
| Warranty extension | +75–150 bps of premium revenue, actuarially reserved | From premium refresh | Premium price realization |
| Retail program | Fund-neutral: reallocate existing co-op from discounts to sell-through programs | Month 3 onward | Reallocation |

**Sequencing logic:** restructuring cash release *precedes* major fighter spend by design. Fighter funds are released in tranches tied to Gate 1 and pilot results — the board never writes one check. **Downside case:** if volume falls a further 10% and cash release lags, the response is to *sequence harder* (accelerate footprint actions, delay fighter category expansion) — not to starve the pilot, which would strand the spend already made. Program target: cash-positive by month 24–30. If the board is unwilling to fund a 2–4% envelope, the honest alternative is the acquisition path, not a half-funded organic build.

## 7. Capability Plan: The Two Execution Risks the Strategy Cannot Wave Away

**Digital/DTC capability — the single largest execution risk.** We are proposing to beat an online-native competitor in a channel where we have no demonstrated capability. Phase 1 must include: hire a DTC general manager and performance-marketing lead *from* e-commerce categories (not promoted from within); contract a 3PL with appliance-grade parcel/LTL delivery and reverse logistics; stand up marketplace operations (Amazon) in Phase 1 using existing entry-level SKUs as a low-cost learning ground before the fighter launches; assemble an agency stack for launch. If the month-12 capability review shows the build lagging, Pivot B (acquire the capability) triggers.

**Footprint adjustment — treated as the major organizational event it is.** Right-sizing likely means plant consolidation and labor relations, not a clause in a cost list. Commission the footprint study in Phase 1 with explicit criteria (sustained utilization below ~70%, fighter sourcing decisions); engage unions/works councils early with no surprises; prioritize redeployment into fighter-brand production where feasible — "same factories, two missions" is both an efficiency and the cultural narrative. Sequence any closure announcements to avoid colliding with the fighter launch and the engineering culture work.

## 8. Sequencing

**Phase 1 (0–6 months): Diagnose, stabilize, bridge.** Decompose the price gap; segment the customer base; run win/loss and WTP analysis. **Bridge actions to stop near-term bleed** (the original plan's gap): sharpen opening price points within the current line; put existing entry SKUs on marketplaces; targeted promotions in the most price-sensitive categories; a certified-refurbished outlet channel; retail price-match support on hero SKUs tied to volume and data commitments. Launch SKU rationalization and design-to-value pilots. Charter the fighter team; make the DTC hires. Hold the retail partner summit and *stop the concession spiral*. Commission the footprint study. Communicate internally: "two missions, one company."

**Gate 1 (day 120–150):** proceed / Pivot A / Pivot B, per Section 3 criteria.

**Phase 2 (6–18 months): Build and launch.** Pilot the fighter online in one or two categories where the disruptor is strongest. Refresh premium around warranty leadership and TCO. Roll out the retail program. Execute footprint decisions. Launch the B2B service pilot for landlords/builders.

**Gate 2 (pilot + two quarters):** scale / adjust / stop on: target cost hit, CAC within threshold, return rates at or below premium line, cannibalization <25%, warranty claims within actuarial assumptions.

**Phase 3 (18–36 months): Scale.** Extend categories only through Gate 2 results. Scale the service model if the B2B pilot's unit economics hold. Revisit M&A if the organic build lags.

## 9. Competitive Dynamics: War-Game the Response

The competitor is not static; the strategy must not be either.

| Scenario | Trigger signal | Pre-agreed response |
|---|---|---|
| Disruptor cuts price further | Sub-cost pricing; funding announcements | Do **not** chase below our cost floor. Compete on availability, service, retail floor presence; monitor their burn rate and funding runway |
| Disruptor moves upmarket | Mid-tier SKUs, feature additions | Collision course — accelerate premium differentiation; hold fighter guardrails rather than letting it drift up to meet them |
| Disruptor acquired by a major player | M&A rumor/announcement | Their capability gap closes — accelerate our timeline; activate our own M&A option on value-tier assets |
| Disruptor enters physical retail | Retailer meetings, listing data | Their channel economics worsen; sharpen retail-exclusive SKUs and the service story |
| Retailer private-label push | PL sourcing RFPs, concession escalation | See Section 10 — make our exclusive-SKU offer structurally more attractive than PL ownership |

## 10. Bringing Retail Partners Along

Retailers don't fundamentally want lower prices — they want **traffic and margin per square foot**. Blanket concessions buy them margin this quarter and a weaker vendor next year. The package instead:

- **Fighter-brand retail-exclusive SKUs** at sharp price points — their showroom-floor answer to the online disruptor.
- **Price-policy discipline, legally structured.** In the US, a unilateral Minimum *Advertised* Price policy (governing advertised, not resale, price) is defensible; in the EU/UK, resale price maintenance is prohibited — use selective distribution criteria, recommended prices, and co-op fund conditionality instead. Per-market legal review before rollout; do not promise retailers "no online undercutting" in jurisdictions where we cannot lawfully deliver it.
- **Exclusive premium models and features** that can't be comparison-shopped online.
- **Co-op funds shifted from discounts to sell-through-linked programs**, plus floor-sales training on the durability/TCO story.
- **Quantified service economics**: put a number on what our durability saves them in returns and warranty handling.
- **Anticipate the private-label countermove.** Retailers demanding concessions have a second lever the plan must address: owning the value tier themselves (the Insignia model). Our exclusive-SKU offer is structured to be more attractive than PL ownership — we carry …[truncated]

There's a version of this plan that begins with platforms and budgets. I'd still start somewhere quieter: with the phone call you already received. The anger, I'd suggest, was less about the web store existing and more about discovering it. Buyers punish surprises; they negotiate strategies. That distinction shapes everything below — but this version of the plan also carries the parts the first draft gestured at without building: the acquisition engine, the unit economics, and the decision rules written down before they're needed.

**Working assumptions** (stated plainly, each with its adjustment path, so the plan commits rather than hedges):

- **A1 — The category is replenishable**, with a 30–90 day repurchase cycle. Subscriptions and replenishment CRM are therefore viable. *If wrong:* pivot the retention engine to loyalty and cross-sell; subscriptions become a membership program instead.
- **A2 — Hero SKUs are promotion-dependent at the two big partners** (typically 30–40% of volume on deal in consumer goods). Assortment separation is therefore essential, and DTC never touches hero-SKU pricing. *If wrong* (i.e., everyday-low-price partners), the pricing doctrine matters less and the assortment separation carries the full weight.
- **A3 — The buyer's call was primarily a process grievance** — the discourtesy of surprise — with margin concern underneath. The transparency doctrine and pricing guardrails address both. *If the deeper fear was data ownership,* the insight-sharing program (§8) is the answer. The plan holds under all three readings.
- **A4 — Company scale supports a $4–6M annual DTC investment at under 1% of revenue.** Adjust absolute figures proportionally; the ratios are the point.

## 1. Strategic posture

Four principles, offered as the spine:

- **Addition, not substitution.** DTC must grow the category and the brand, not reroute the same shopper's same trip. Every SKU and campaign passes one test: *could a buyer read about this in a trade publication and shrug?*
- **Transparency over stealth.** The pilot taught us that hiding is the actual provocation. The retailers hear everything from us first — strategically framed, but first.
- **Price discipline as doctrine.** We never undercut retail. Guardrails we write ourselves are cheaper than guardrails written for us.
- **Data as diplomacy.** First-party data gets *shared* — curated, but shared — and, more powerfully, gets *used on the retailers' behalf* (§8), so the channel looks like a gift to the people funding us.

## 2. Channel architecture

| Layer | Role | Conflict exposure |
|---|---|---|
| **Brand.com flagship** | Exclusive assortment, bundles, subscriptions, content, community | Low, if assortment is differentiated (§4) |
| **Packaging layer (QR on pack)** | Converts *retail* shoppers into known consumers via content, loyalty, registration | Moderate — see §8; sophisticated buyers understand exactly what this builds, and we should plan on that |
| **Experiential (pop-ups, events)** | Brand theater + data capture in flagship markets | Low — trivial volume, shared PR value |
| **Partner-aligned digital** | Retailer .com dropship, retail media co-investment, "where to buy" referral links on brand.com | Negative — actively feeds the partners |
| **Marketplaces (Amazon etc.)** | First-party entry deliberately deferred | See brand-protection note below |

**Marketplace deferral with eyes open.** Deferring Amazon does not defer Amazon: unauthorized resellers and gray-market sellers will fill the vacuum, and the resulting price erosion will anger our retail partners anyway — through a channel we don't control. So while first-party entry waits, brand protection starts in Phase 0: Brand Registry enrollment, a unilateral authorized-reseller and MAP policy (counsel-reviewed), automated monitoring of unauthorized listings and price erosion, and periodic test buys to trace diversion. Pre-committed revisit trigger: if gray-market listings persistently price >10% below MSRP or dominate the category page, a disciplined official presence becomes the *lesser* evil — stabilizing prices is something we can credibly present to partners as done partly on their behalf.

**Fulfillment:** a 3PL, variable-cost, so that if we ever need to slow down, no fixed cost base is stranded.

## 3. Product and pricing differentiation

The cleanest resolution of channel conflict is assortment that doesn't overlap in any meaningful way:

| Assortment layer | Retail | DTC |
|---|---|---|
| Hero / weekly-promo SKUs | Theirs, untouched | Absent, or listed at full MSRP and never promoted |
| Core range | Full | Limited representation at MSRP — convenience, not competition |
| Bundles, kits, gifting | — | Exclusive configurations that don't exist at retail |
| Limited editions, collabs, drops | Occasional co-created *retail* exclusives | DTC-first drops |
| Personalization / engraving | — | Exclusive |
| Long-tail, legacy, discontinued SKUs | Won't carry | Exclusive

# Monetization Strategy: Revenue Growth Without Retention Damage

## 1. Diagnosis and Design Principles

**Why conversion is stuck below 2%:** A single paid tier against a heterogeneous user base is a pricing mismatch, not a monetization-proof audience. Some users would pay more than you're asking; most will never pay your current price but would pay *something*; a large group will never pay at all and must be monetized differently. One price captures almost none of this.

**Why past tests backfired:** Both failures were *mechanism* failures, not monetization failures. Hard paywalls **subtracted** value users already had. Intrusive ads **taxed attention indiscriminately**, including users on a path to paying. Everything below is built on addition and alignment instead.

**Five design principles (every tactic follows these):**

1. **Grandfather everything that exists today.** Nothing free users have now is removed, degraded, capped, or ad-supported. All monetization is additive. (This constrains usage-based pricing to *new* capabilities only — see §2B.)
2. **Monetize intensity, not access.** Charge the users who extract the most value; keep the front door wide open.
3. **Match the mechanism to the segment.** Subscriptions for habitual users, metering for heavy users of new capabilities, ads only for predicted never-payers, partnerships where they add value.
4. **Every surface is an experiment with a kill switch.** Nothing ships to 100% without clearing guardrails — and guardrails must be measurable at the cell size we're actually running (see §7 on power).
5. **Cap total monetization pressure per user.** A per-segment budget on prompts, impressions, and upsell surfaces, so no user experiences the app "turning into a billboard."

---

## 2. The Monetization Mix (with justification)

Target 18–24 month net revenue mix: **~65% subscriptions, ~8% usage-based, ~15% advertising, ~12% partnerships.** (Usage-based is deliberately smaller than instinct suggests — see §2B for why.)

### A. Restructured subscription tiers — the primary engine

| Tier | Price (gross, illustrative) | Net of store fees* | Contents | Target |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Free** | $0 | — | Everything users have today, unchanged, unmetered | Everyone |
| **Plus** | $6.99/mo | ~$5.70 | Convenience: sync, offline, customization, quality-of-life | Habitual users |
| **Pro** | $14.99/mo | ~$12.30 | Capability: advanced tools, automation, priority support, early access, generous allowances on *new* metered features | Power users |

*\*App-store economics are material and must be in every revenue figure: 30% standard fee, 15% under small-business programs and for year-2+ subscriptions on iOS. Assume a blended ~18% at your scale; use net prices in all targets. Where feasible, offer web billing to recover margin, within store rules.*

**Justification:** Tiering captures heterogeneous willingness to pay a single tier cannot. Pro anchors Plus as "reasonable," lifting mid-tier conversion. The gate sits on *enhancements and new capability*, never on existing free functionality — the direct fix for the paywall backlash. Add **annual plans at ~2 months free**: immediate cash (investor optics) and structurally lower churn via reduced renewal frequency. Add **regional pricing** — at millions of users you are certainly leaving money on the table in lower-WTP markets; regional pricing also reduces the temptation to run risky price A/B tests (§7).

### B. Usage-based pricing — new capabilities only, hybrid, never pure

**Resolving the grandfathering tension explicitly:** metering applies **only to capabilities launched after the restructure** (e.g., new AI features, expanded storage tiers, premium exports). Anything free and unmetered today stays free and unmetered, permanently. Capping an existing free feature *is* a paywall — that is the mechanism that spiked uninstalls, and it is off the table.

The honest consequence: usage-based revenue ramps slowly, because it depends on adoption of features that don't exist yet. Model it as a month-12+ lever contributing ~8% of revenue at steady state, not a near-term fix. Do not let investor pressure push metering onto existing features — that trades the core asset (retention) for the fastest-available dollar.

Mechanics: **soft monthly allowances + optional top-ups.** Free gets a genuinely useful allowance on new features; Plus gets more; Pro gets a lot; anyone can buy a top-up pack *without subscribing*. This captures high-intensity, subscription-averse users and aligns revenue with cost-to-serve. Pure metered billing is rejected — bill anxiety is corrosive in consumer.

### C. Advertising — narrowly scoped, propensity-gated, opt-in by design

- **Only users below a payer-propensity threshold see ads.** "Never-payer" is a prediction, not a fact. Build a conversion-propensity model; show ads only to users in the **bottom band** of predicted WTP. **Exclude the borderline middle band entirely** — the cost of suppressing one future subscriber exceeds years of their ad ARPU.
- **Rewarded and native formats only**: user opts in to watch in exchange for credits, temporary premium, or unlocks. No interstitials, no forced video, nothing in core task flows.
- **New-user cohorts first**; existing users grandfathered ad-free or explicitly opt in for perks.
- Hard frequency caps, strict ad-quality vetting, no data-broker networks.
- **Compliance is a design input, not an afterthought:** plan for ATT opt-in rates of ~25–35% on iOS (model non-consenting users as contextual-only, at lower eCPM), a GDPR consent-management platform, and in-app-bidding mediation. Set a **build/no-build threshold**: if projected net ad ARPDAU across the addressable pool falls below ~$0.008, the ads line isn't worth the engineering and ratings risk — partnerships absorb that segment instead.
- **Segment migration rule:** when an ad-exposed casual user crosses into habitual behavior (e.g., 3+ sessions/week for 3 consecutive weeks), ads stop within 7 days and the user moves to the Plus upsell track. No user should ever experience "graduated into engagement, still being taxed with ads."

**Justification:** This monetizes the segment with near-zero willingness to pay. Interruption caused the past ratings damage; *chosen* ads in exchange for value historically rate far better. The propensity gate and migration rule fix the misclassification risk the naive version creates.

### D. Partnerships — the zero-attention-tax revenue, done properly

Partnerships were the thinnest lever in the prior plan; here is the full treatment, prioritized by UX safety:

1. **B2B2C bundles (primary).** A partner (telco, bank, device maker, employer-perks platform) pays for Plus/Pro as *their* perk. Zero consumer UX cost, prepaid revenue, and built-in distribution. Target: 1–2 deals by month 12.
2. **Contextual affiliate/commerce.** Offers surfaced only where genuinely relevant to in-app intent. **Revenue model: flat placement fee or rev-share, not pure CPA** — pure CPA incentivizes you to spam, recreating the ads problem through a different door.
3. **Co-marketing and integrations.** Distribution swaps that cost nothing and may drive acquisition.

**Partner selection criteria:** measured audience overlap, brand-safety screen, and a relevance bar validated by pilot CTR *and* zero retention delta in the exposed cohort. **Quality guardrails per partner surface:** complaint rate, uninstall-within-24h-of-exposure, and NPS delta vs. holdout (§8). One spammy integration gets the whole program paused — that is the standing rule, stated to partners up front.

---

## 3. The Revenue Model: Demonstrating "Meaningful"

The request demands meaningfully higher revenue per user. Here is the arithmetic, with assumptions stated so they can be re-based to your actuals.

**Illustrative baseline:** 5M MAU, ~1M DAU, 1.8% paying $8/mo blended gross.
90k subs × $8 × 0.82 (blended fees) ≈ **$590k/mo net ≈ $7.1M/yr. Net ARPDAU ≈ $0.019.**

**Base case at month 18–24:**

| Line | Build-up | Net $/mo |
|---|---|---|
| Plus | 125k subs (2.5% of MAU) × $5.70 | $713k |
| Pro | 50k subs (1.0% of MAU) × $12.30 | $615k |
| Usage top-ups | New-feature adoption: ~35k buyers × $3.50 avg | $120k |
| Ads | ~1.6M addressable casual users post-propensity-filter and consent; blended net ad ARPDAU $0.012 across ~450k exposed DAU | $160k |
| Partnerships | One B2B2C bundle (100k subs × $1.50) + affiliate | $200k |
| **Total** | **3.5% of MAU paying + non-sub lines** | **~$1.81M/mo ≈ $21.7M/yr** |

**Net ARPDAU: $0.019 → ~$0.060, a ~3.2× increase. Blended free→paid conversion 1.8% → 3.5%** (within freemium norms of 2–5%).

**Sensitivity:**

| Scenario | Key assumption shifts | Net revenue vs. baseline |
|---|---|---|
| Conservative | 2.6% conversion, ads below build threshold (dropped), partnerships at half | ~1.9× |
| Base | As above | ~3.2× |
| Upside | 4.2% conversion, second bundle deal, top-ups at 2× | ~4.6× |

**Honesty about the loss gap:** if current net burn is roughly $1–1.5M/mo, the base case closes most of it by month 18–24; the conservative case does not, and implies cost action must run in parallel. Do not present the upside case to investors — present the base case with the holdout as the credibility mechanism (§9). A plan that only works at upside is how the previous paywall decision got made.

---

## 4. Segment → Offer Map

*Behavioral archetypes below — validate against your clustering (recency, frequency, depth, feature breadth) and confirm per-segment WTP with Van Westendorp or conjoint before Phase 2.*

| Segment (behavioral) | ~Share | Value they get | Primary offer | Secondary | Explicitly avoid |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Casual/occasional** — <2 sessions/wk, single feature | 60–70% | Utility on demand | Rewarded ads **only if bottom-band propensity** | Relevant partner offers | Paywalls, pushy upsell, forced ads |
| **Habitual engaged** — daily/weekly, multi-feature | 20–30% | Routine, embedded in life | **Plus** subscription | Free trial triggered at value moments | Ads in core flows |
| **Power users** — top 5–10% by depth | 5–10% | Near-professional value | **Pro** + annual | Top-ups on new features, status perks | Any feature removal or cap on existing features |
| **At-risk / declining** — engagement trending down | varies | Fading | **Nothing.** Win-back flows only | — | All monetization pressure (it accelerates churn) |
| **Creators/earners** *(if applicable)* | small | Income/reach via platform | Revenue share / take rate | Pro tools | Opaque fee changes |

**Migration rules between segments** (previously unspecified, now explicit):
- Casual → habitual: ads cease within 7 days; user enters Plus track; ad exposure history is logged so we can measure whether prior ad exposure suppressed conversion.
- Habitual → at-risk: all upsell prompts suppressed immediately.
- Any segment → paying: all ads cease permanently at first payment.

**Prompt placement rule across all segments:** upgrade asks appear only at moments of *realized value* — after an aha moment, when hitting a soft limit on a *new* feature, when using a feature adjacent to premium. Never at app open, never mid-task.

---

## 5. Existing Paid Base: Migration Plan (previously missing)

The current ~2% of payers are the highest-LTV users and the most dangerous to mishandle. Tier restructures routinely cause downgrade-driven revenue dilution and backlash among legacy subscribers. Plan:

1. **Feature match, never feature loss.** Every legacy subscriber is mapped to the tier that contains *everything they have today*. If the new ladder splits their features across tiers, they get the higher tier.
2. **Price honored for 12 months minimum.** Legacy subscribers keep their current price on their mapped tier for a year; increases require 60 days' notice and apply only at renewal.
3. **Upgrade incentive, not pressure.** One-time offer to move to Pro at a discounted annual rate or with top-up credits. Single prompt, dismissible, never repeated.
4. **Dedicated guardrails** (added to §8): legacy-subscriber downgrade rate, legacy support-ticket rate, involuntary churn during migration windows.
5. **Model the dilution honestly:** expect 5–10% of legacy subs to downgrade to Plus at the lower price. This is already reflected in the §3 build-up (Plus count includes migrated downgraders); if observed dilution exceeds 10%, revisit the Plus/Pro feature split.

---

## 6. Retention-Side Levers (protecting revenue actively, not just avoiding harm)

Retention protection is not only defensive. These fit the "addition, not subtraction" philosophy and each recovers revenue that would otherwise silently churn:

- **Save offers at cancel:** a cancel-flow screen offering a pause, a downgrade to Plus, or a limited-time discount — in that order, since pause preserves the relationship and downgrade preserves revenue.
- **Pause option (1–3 months):** standard in consumer subscriptions; converts cancels into resumes.
- **Graceful downgrade paths:** Pro → Plus preserves all data, settings, and history; nothing is deleted on downgrade, only gated. A user who downgrades and stays is worth far more than one who churns from a bad downgrade experience.
- **Win-back pricing for churned subscribers:** a single, time-limited reactivation offer at 30/60/90 days post-churn, then silence. Win-back of a former payer is cheaper than converting a never-payer.
- **At-risk segment value reinforcement:** proactive surfacing of unused high-value features — retention work, not monetization, per the segment map.

---

## 7. Experiment Plan

### Phases

**Phase 0 — Instrumentation (weeks 0–6).** No user-facing changes. Cohort dashboards, uninstall attribution, review-scraping, per-surface kill switches, consent-management platform, propensity model v1. Finalize segments and WTP research. Set baselines; pre-register thresholds and power calculations.

**Phase 1 — Lowest-regret launches (weeks 6–14).** Rewarded ads to 5–10% of *new*, bottom-band-propensity casual users (geo-clustered A/B vs. holdout). One B2B2C partnership pilot. These touch no existing user workflows and generate early revenue signal.

**Phase 2 — Tier restructure (weeks 10–24).** Launch Plus/Pro to 5% of eligible traffic with explicit grandfathering messaging; legacy migration begins in parallel per §5. Scale 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% with gated checkpoints (below).

**Phase 3 — Usage-based add-ons (weeks 20–32).** Launch the *new* metered capabilities first; allowances and top-ups follow adoption. Test allowance sizes (too tight recreates the paywall problem on new features; too loose leaves revenue).

**Phase 4 — Scale and iterate.** Roll winners to full population; quarterly price/packaging review.

### Experiment design rules (substantially revised)

- **Price tests: geography, not individuals.** Showing different prices to comparable users in the same market invites screenshots, PR backlash, and app-store scrutiny. Instead: (a) randomize price at the **country/region level**; (b) prefer **packaging tests** (vary feature composition at a fixed price) over price tests — packaging differences are defensible, price differences are screenshot-able; (c) test new price points only on **new SKUs** where no anchor exists. Never run two prices for the same SKU in the same market.
- **Spillover control.** Users talk, so user-level randomization on visible monetization (prices, ads) risks contamination. Use **cluster-level randomization** (geo or, where the social graph is dense, community-detection clusters) for ads and pricing; reserve user-level randomization for invisible-to-others surfaces (prompt copy, placement). Measure contamination directly: monitor holdout users' exposure via support tickets and social mentions.

# Monetization Strategy — Revised Draft (v2)

A note before the plan: we are grateful for the careful critique of the first draft. The spine survives — monetize **new value, heavy usage, and willing attention**, never the existing core loop — but the economics have been rebuilt with stated assumptions, the internal tensions are resolved rather than asserted away, and several missing pieces (a sufficiency target, existing-subscriber migration, governance) are now included. Where a decision properly belongs to finance or leadership, we frame it as a proposal for their calibration rather than a conclusion.

---

## 1. Success Criteria Before Tactics (the sufficiency check)

The brief's binding constraint is investor patience, so "meaningfully increases revenue" must be defined before we design toward it. We would propose leadership and finance set the target explicitly; the framework below is offered to structure that conversation.

**Illustrative scenario at 5M MAU** (scale linearly to actual figures):

| | Today | Month 18 (planning case) |
|---|---|---|
| Blended net ARPU/mo | ~$0.09–0.10 | ~$0.20–0.30 |
| Annualized net revenue | ~$5.5–6M | ~$12–18M |

All figures **net of platform fees** (15–30%; we model 20–25% blended, improving with small-business programs, second-year subscription rates, and — where permitted — web billing, which saves fees but adds friction and should be tested, not assumed).

Whether this suffices depends on the burn, and we should say so honestly:

| Annual net burn | Strategy covers | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| $10M | Fully, with runway extension | Monetization alone may suffice |
| $20M | ~60–90% | Pair with modest cost discipline |
| $40M | ~30–45% | Monetization buys time; the cost structure must also move |

An illustrative commitment for the board's consideration: **reduce net burn by ≥50% within 18 months**, calibrated once finance confirms the actual loss position. Better to surface a shortfall in this document than in month twelve.

---

## 2. Guiding Principles (one clarification)

1. **Grandfather everything** — defined precisely: *no degradation of any experience a user has today.* New features, and usage limits set above current behavior, are monetizable. This clarification matters: it is the only way existing users can ever be converted, and it makes the premium pipeline in Section 5 a requirement, not a nicety.
2. Charge in proportion to value received.
3. Ads only as opt-in value exchange, never as a tax.
4. Test on new users first.
5. Every experiment ships with a pre-registered kill switch — and a named owner (Section 9).

---

## 3. Segmentation — a Hypothesis, Held Loosely

We expect behavioral clustering (frequency, breadth, depth, recency) to return **three to five groups**; the four archetypes below are a working template, not a prediction. The offer map is keyed to *behavioral signatures* rather than names, so if the data returns a different structure, offers re-attach to signatures without redesigning the portfolio.

| Segment (working hypothesis) | Signature | Monetization posture |
|---|---|---|
| Devotees (~5–10%) | Daily, deep, advanced features | Charge confidently |
| Regulars (~20–30%) | Weekly+ core loop | Convert via new value and convenience |
| Casuals (~40–60%) | Occasional, single-feature | Consented attention + small purchases; never gate |
| Passers-by | Dormant/churning | No monetization surface; they write the 1-star reviews |

---

## 4. The Portfolio — Corrected Economics, Resolved Tensions

### 4.1 Subscriptions (the spine) — with the conversion mechanism spelled out

**Plus** ($4.99–5.99/mo): convenience tier. **Pro** ($9.99–14.99/mo): capability tier. These anchors sit within the ranges mainstream consumer freemium apps cluster in (entry ~$4–8, premium ~$10–20 across adjacent categories), and will be validated by Van Westendorp and conjoint before locking.

The earlier draft asserted 2% → 3.5–4% without a mechanism. Here is the path, each step independently testable:

1. **New-user onboarding presentation** — new users carry no entitlement loss; this is where conversion is won, and likely the largest single driver.
2. **Free trial with opt-in reminders** (reminders protect ratings and reduce refunds).
3. **Annual-first presentation** (2 months free) — cash flow and structurally lower churn.
4. **Regional and student pricing** — willingness-to-pay varies more by geography than most pricing pages admit.
5. **Win-back and downgrade-save offers.**
6. **Premium pipeline cadence** (Section 5) — launch moments create natural, non-coercive upsell surfaces.

Planning assumptions: blended payer ARPU $6.50–7.50 gross (mix ~70–75% Plus / 25–30% Pro; 40–50% annual). We plan conservatively on **2.5% blended conversion by month 12, aspiring to 3–3.5% by month 18** — higher among new-user cohorts, slower in the existing base.

### 4.2 Usage-based pricing — one currency, no double-charging

The first draft created a collision: credit packs sold to Devotees in Phase 1 for the same actions Pro would later bundle. Resolution: **credits are the single metering currency across the app.**

- Pro **includes** a monthly allotment sized to typical Pro usage; packs are the overage mechanism for everyone, including Pro users.
- Steady users should find Pro better value than packs — that is the intended upgrade path, not an accident.
- Phase 1 credit buyers: balances honored indefinitely, plus a Pro trial at launch. No one is charged twice for the same value.
- A free monthly allotment for all users, with paid limits set **above the current 99th-percentile usage**, ensures no existing behavior is taxed.

### 4.3 Advertising — smaller, cleaner, compliant

The earlier ad math was too optimistic; we recalibrate with stated assumptions: 20–30% opt-in among Casuals; engaged opt-ins average 8–20 rewarded views/month (hard cap 1/day); blended net eCPM $6–12 (iOS lower post-ATT; modeled conservatively). That yields **$0.05–0.24 per opted-in user per month, or ~$0.01–0.05 blended; planning case $0.02–0.03.**

Two further corrections:

- **Reward design:** rewards grant **credits (consumables), not subscription time.** The earlier "day of Plus" idea risked teaching the most price-sensitive segment that premium is free with patience — quietly undermining the Plus impulse-conversion goal. A Plus day-pass may be tested later, but only as a measured experiment under the cannibalization guardrail below.
- **Compliance and quality (also ratings protection):** consent management (GDPR/CCPA), ATT-aware iOS assumptions, mediation with category blocklists and content-adjacency screening, **under-18s excluded from ads entirely**, no ads near sensitive content.

### 4.4 Partnership

results.finalResponse:
Reading between the lines of this situation, two things stand out before any plan gets written. First, the customers aren't attached to the legacy product — they're attached to a handful of capabilities. That makes this a *capability continuity* program wearing the clothes of a product EOL, and it's worth treating it that way. Second, the real deadline probably isn't the security curve or the maintenance bill. It's the retirement dates on a short list of engineers. So the timeline below is *derived from* the knowledge map rather than imposed on it — if Phase 0 tells us the people clock runs faster than the dates assume, the dates move, not the people plan.

And one thing worth saying plainly before the mechanics: with a third of company profit sitting on this product, "should we sunset at all?" is a question the board will ask whether we answer it or not. Better that we arrive with the answer already in hand.

Dates and figures throughout are proposals for the steering group to ratify, not doctrine — the assumptions are where I'd welcome pushback.

---

## 0. Strategic options — confirm sunset is the right answer

Before committing the organization, it's worth documenting the comparison honestly, so the decision is seen as chosen rather than assumed:

| Option | What it means | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Sunset with structured migration** (recommended) | EOL the legacy platform; rebuild critical capabilities; migrate customers | Protects relationships and pulls revenue onto the strategic platform; highest execution burden |
| **B. Divest to a specialty maintenance firm** | Sell the product line and its customer base | Generates cash but strands the most loyal customers mid-dependency, hands competitors a narrative, and forfeits the migration upside; the buyer inherits the same knowledge cliff |
| **C. License codebase / outsource maintenance** | Third party maintains legacy under our brand or theirs | A useful *fallback* for the long tail; as the primary strategy it keeps security liability near us while control moves away |
| **D. Re-invest and extend life** | Modernize the legacy stack | Rejected: rebuilds yesterday's architecture at tomorrow's prices, and the retiring knowledge base can't be rehired |

**Recommendation: A**, with C held in reserve for die-hard tail accounts at hard stop. **Revisit trigger:** if the Phase 0 audit shows parity rebuild is infeasible for a block representing more than ~20% of legacy ARR, bring option B back to the steering group for that segment rather than forcing an impossible rebuild.

## 1. Success targets and retention economics — set these before anything else

Walk-away decisions made ad hoc under pressure tend to go badly, so the numbers should be agreed early, collectively, and calmly:

- **Retention targets:** ≥90% of Tier 1 ARR migrated or committed by month 36; ≥85% of total legacy ARR; ≥70% of the long tail. No more than 2 of the top-20 watchlist accounts lost to a competitor (customers who retire the workload entirely are a different, gentler outcome).
- **"Committed," defined:** a signed migration plan with a target date and a named executive sponsor on both sides, a contract amendment embedding migration, or a co-funding agreement. Verbal intent is encouraging but does not count.
- **Program budget cap:** total program spend — tooling, incentives, co-funded engineering, retention bonuses, dual-run cost — held to roughly 15–20% of three-year legacy gross profit, tracked monthly by a finance partner on the core team.
- **Walk-away rule:** per-account retention spend (credits + co-funded engineering + services) capped at ~30% of that account's expected three-year post-migration gross profit. Above that, the decision goes to the steering committee, and the default answer becomes a graceful exit.
- **Credit sizing rationale:** the 10–15% migration credit below is calibrated to offset roughly half of a typical account's migration services cost, and in all cases to stay below one year of that account's gross margin — cheaper than churn, not so generous it invites gaming.

## 2. Phase 0 — Quiet preparation (Months 0–6, pre-announcement)

Resist the urge to announce early. Six months of groundwork first:

- **Dependency audit, sequenced Tier-1-first.** Instrument or survey to learn which niche features are *actually used*, by whom, and how deeply — starting with watchlist accounts in the first 90 days, so parity scoping is real by briefing time. Legacy platforms often lack telemetry; a lightweight assessment agent plus support-ticket mining gets most of the way. There's a real gap between what customers say they need and what their workflows touch.
- **Pilot migration wave.** Two or three friendly accounts — cooperative, mid-complexity, representative — begin migrating under NDA during Phase 0. Gate criteria before general rollout: ≥99.5% data reconciliation fidelity, rollback demonstrated, cutover downtime within target. The pilot validates the tooling, surfaces data-model edge cases while the legacy experts are still available to explain them, and produces two referenceable stories by announcement day.
- **Account risk scoring and tiering.** Niche-feature dependency × switching cost × renewal timing × viable alternatives × relationship health. **Tier 1:** roughly the top 20 accounts, ~40–50% of legacy ARR, deep dependency or ecosystem influence. **Tier 2:** the next 30–40% of ARR. **Tier 3:** the remainder.
- **Knowledge map and coverage floor.** Who knows what, and when do they leave? Define the floor explicitly: every critical subsystem covered by at least two qualified engineers, or one plus a named emeritus advisor. This floor, not preference, sets the outer boundary of the timeline.
- **Contract, regulatory, and data-retention review.** Perpetual licenses, SLAs, government commitments, license-server dependencies, and customers' regulatory obligations to keep legacy data readable (often 7+ years). Better to find out now.
- **Ecosystem and OEM inventory.** Who has the legacy product embedded in their own offering? Which ISVs and integrators build on it? They cannot migrate on the standard timeline and need their own track (Section 5).
- **Internal impact assessment.** The legacy support and operations org will hear "EOL" too. Retention and redeployment plans for them belong in Phase 0, before anyone starts quietly job-hunting.
- **Security baseline.** Third-party audit so the exposure trajectory is documented, not anecdotal.

## 3. Sunset timeline and support policy

Anchor on ~36 months from announcement to end of support, with a hard outer boundary set by physics (people, unpatchable dependencies), not preference. **Derivation rule:** hard stop falls at the earlier of 48 months, or the date the knowledge map projects the coverage floor breaks, minus a six-month buffer. Stress-test quarterly against actual departures.

| Milestone | Timing (from announcement) | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| End of sale | Immediate | No new legacy contracts; expansions by exception only |
| Maintenance mode | Months 0–24 | Critical/high security patches + Sev-1 fixes only; no enhancements, no new environment certifications |
| Final migration window (limited support) | Months 24–36 | Critical security patches only; Sev-1 handled via workarounds rather than code fixes; the support story is now migration assistance |
| End of support (EOL) | Month 36 | Standard support ends |
| Extended support | Months 36–48 | Paid, critical-security-only, best-effort — *available only to customers with a signed migration plan* |
| Hard stop | Month 48 | All support and patch eligibility end; archives, documentation, and escrow remain |

Design choices worth noting:

- **Gates alongside dates.** Track coverage gates (40% of legacy ARR migrated or committed by month 12, 70% by month 24, 85% by month 30). Hold **one** pre-committed 6-month extension lever, decided at the month-24 gate review by the steering committee (program lead, CPO, CRO, CFO) on defined evidence: ARR committed below 60%, material Tier-1 accounts unsigned, *and* the coverage floor intact. Announced once, never twice — beyond that, extended support absorbs stragglers rather than moving the date. Credibility of the timeline is itself a migration tool.
- **Escalating extended-support pricing** (e.g., 20% of contract value in year one, 30% in year two). The price curve should tell the story the dates tell.
- **One firm rule:** no new features on legacy, ever. Every exception extends the tail.
- **What "hard stop" legally means.** For hosted customers, the service ends. For on-prem perpetual licenses, the software keeps running — what ends is support, patch eligibility, and indemnification. Say so explicitly in every contract and communication; issue perpetual offline license keys and place license-server functionality in escrow so no customer's operations depend on our infrastructure surviving. The plan should never be read as "we disable your software."
- **When a Tier 1 simply pays full price and refuses to sign a migration plan:** rather than a flat refusal, offer per-incident support at premium time-and-materials rates — no SLA, with a written security-risk acknowledgment. This prices the risk honestly, keeps the relationship warm, and quietly makes migration the sensible path. Going forward, renewal language embeds the migration-plan expectation, so leverage builds with each cycle.

## 4. Niche capabilities: rebuild, bridge, or retire

Score each feature on four axes: revenue attached

# Monetization Architecture: Capturing Value Without Spending Retention

**Revision 2 — prepared for circulation, not for immediate decision**

*A note on how I'd like this read. This is a proposal I would want to walk through with Growth, Finance, Support, Data, and Legal before anything is put in front of the board or the investors. Several of the numbers below are mine to defend, but several are placeholders where another team owns the truth, and I've marked those clearly rather than quietly assuming. Where I've made a call, I've shown the reasoning so that colleagues who see it differently can point at the specific step they'd change rather than having to disagree with the whole document.*

*One thing I'd ask us to hold onto as we discuss the past tests: the paywall and ad experiments were reasonable bets made with the information available, and the people who ran them gave us the two most useful data points we own. I'd very much prefer we treat those results as shared learning. A monetization program that starts by assigning fault will not get the honest telemetry it needs from the teams closest to the users.*

*Convention used throughout: `[A]` marks an **assumption** I believe but have not verified; `[D]` marks a **diagnostic** we must run before the number is meaningful; `[O]` marks an item where **another function owns the answer** and I've left a placeholder.*

---

## 0. Executive summary in one page

| | Today | Q1 exit | Q4 exit (M12) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gross consumer spend per MAU / mo | $0.16 | $0.24 | $0.64 |
| **Net revenue per MAU / mo** (after store fees, refunds) | **$0.115** | **$0.17** | **$0.553** |
| Gross profit per MAU / mo (after COGS) | ~$0.03 | ~$0.09 | ~$0.45 |
| Paid subscription penetration | 2.0% | 2.3% | ~5.3% |
| Revenue lines carrying >30% of total | 1 | 1 | 0 |

The strategy has four moves, deliberately ordered so that the earliest revenue carries the least retention risk:

1. **Fix the leaks before adding pressure** (Q1). Involuntary churn recovery, cancellation save offers, annual-plan migration, web checkout where legally available, affiliate commerce. All of this is additive, none of it is visible to a free user as a new tax, and it is the only part of the plan that lands inside 90 days.
2. **Replace one price with a ladder and a meter** (Q2–Q3). Three subscription tiers plus family, and — the piece I believe is genuinely missing — usage-based pricing for the large episodic segment that will never sign a recurring commitment.
3. **Build a second business quietly** (Q2–Q4, extending beyond). Teams/Business for the commercial users already inside the consumer base; near-term embedded/API partnerships. Revenue that touches no free user's experience at all.
4. **Rebuild the ratings asset, then and only then re-approach advertising** (Q3–Q4). Rewarded and native only, behind hard-coded constraints, gated on a ratings-recovery precondition.

**What I am least confident about, and would want the group to pressure-test:** the 2% → 5.3% penetration bridge (§6), the advertising ARPU assumption given iOS signal loss (§5.4), and whether we have the organizational bandwidth to run this many parallel workstreams without the quality of any one of them slipping.

---

## 1. Before we prescribe: the diagnosis we owe ourselves

I had originally written that the single-tier price structure was the cause of the 2% ceiling. On reflection that was a hypothesis wearing the clothes of a finding, and I'd rather withdraw it than defend it. There are at least four explanations for a 2% conversion rate, and they imply completely different plans:

| Hypothesis | Test | If true, the plan changes to… |
|---|---|---|
| **Exposure** — most users never see a paid offer | Decompose: MAU → paywall impression → trial start → paid → retained M3 | Offer placement and contextual triggering, not pricing. Cheapest fix in the document. |
| **Activation** — users never reach the moment that makes payment rational | Correlate paid conversion with reaching each core value milestone; measure milestone attainment rate | Onboarding and time-to-value work precedes all packaging work |
| **Price/packaging** — the offer is mispriced or mis-fenced for most of the base | WTP study per segment; price-point elasticity | The ladder in §4 |
| **Mechanics** — trial→paid leakage, payment failures, no save path | Billing funnel audit, dunning report, cancellation flow audit | §3, and it's nearly free |

**This decomposition takes roughly two days of analyst time and I would not want us to commit to anything else until it's done.** `[D]` If exposure turns out to be, say, 20% of MAU, then we are converting ~10% of exposed users — which is a healthy offer with a distribution problem, and half of the packaging work below becomes lower priority. I'd rather discover that in week one than in month six.

I've written the rest of the document as though price/packaging and exposure both matter, because that is my prior `[A]`. But the sequencing in §7 is built so that the diagnosis can redirect us without wasting work.

---

## 2. The framing I'd propose we adopt

Both prior tests share a structure worth noticing: they taxed *everyone equally* for value that is *distributed very unequally*. A paywall that lands on a user receiving $40/month of value is a bargain; the same paywall on a user receiving $0.50 of value reads as an insult, and insulted users do not leave quietly — they leave a review.

The working thesis I'd like us to align on: **let each segment pay in the currency it has a surplus of.** Some users have money. Some have attention. Some have time and willingness to contribute. Some have reach. Some sit inside an organization with a budget nobody has ever asked them about. A single-currency model leaves most of that uncollected while irritating everyone.

Two constraints I would treat as non-negotiable, because the uninstall spike already proved the first and the ratings damage proved the second:

1. **Never charge for what a user already has.** We monetize depth, new headroom, and cost-to-serve. Existing habit is grandfathered permanently. The free tier is not charity — it is the distribution engine, the ratings shield, and the top of every funnel beneath it.
2. **Never monetize a user who is already leaving.** More on this in §3.3.

---

## 3. Segment map, offer assignment, and the classification problem

Shares below are my working estimates `[A]`; they sum to 100% and should be replaced by the actual clustering output. Two axes drive the offer assignment: **value received** and **shape of need** (continuous vs. episodic). Subscription fits continuous need; usage-based fits episodic need. Forcing episodic users into subscriptions is, I believe, where consumer apps most reliably manufacture their own churn — and is my best explanation for the earlier uninstall spike.

# Supply Risk Strategy: Critical Precision Component (Revised)

## 1. Executive Summary

**Situation.** Our sole source for a critical precision component has been acquired by a competitor's parent and has since raised prices twice and slipped deliveries. Each event has an innocent explanation; together they warrant preparation, not accusation. Qualification of an alternative takes 18 months — until then, we are dependent, and our order patterns are partially visible to a competitor.

**Strategy.** Run a dual track. **Track A — relationship:** pursue a long-term agreement and executive-level reset with the new parent, conducted so the supplier loses face in nothing and gains a committed customer. **Track B — independence, built quietly:** replicate tooling, qualify two second sources in parallel, build a dynamically sized buffer, and carry redesign and partial vertical integration as gated options. Track B is sized to survive a worst-case cutoff; Track A reduces the probability we ever need it.

**The ask.** (1) Approve a Year-1 budget envelope of **$6–9M** (illustrative; §6 provides the parametric model for calibration). (2) Stand up the Supply Risk Council and gate calendar (§8). (3) Pre-authorize the escalation triggers in §7 so thresholds are decided now, not rationalized later.

---

## 2. Situation Assessment

The risk is now threefold, in ascending order of severity:

1. **Commercial** — price increases at an observed cadence, delivery slippage.
2. **Structural** — single source, unique tooling and tacit know-how, 18-month qualification clock.
3. **Strategic** — volumes, timing, and roadmap signals now flow to an owner with competitive interests.

The 18-month clock governs everything. Each option is judged by whether it *shortens the clock*, *bridges it*, or *removes the need for it*.

---

## 3. Worst-Case Stress Test — the Coverage Gap (addressed head-on)

**Scenario:** hard cutoff at month 4 — supplier stops shipping with minimal notice.

**Exposure at baseline plan:** buffer built to ~2–3 months; second source unqualified until month 18; redesign uncommitted; captive capability nonexistent. **Uncovered gap: ~13 months. The baseline plan fails this test.** Closing the gap requires all four levers below; no single one suffices.

| Lever | Action | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Compress the clock** | Replicate tooling immediately (§5, T-1); qualify **two** candidates in parallel; pre-agree PPAP/first-article plans; dedicate engineering | Qualification 18 → **12–14 months** |
| **2. Size the buffer dynamically** | Coverage target = *(months remaining to qualification) + 2-month margin*, floored at 6 months. Peak target **9–12 months** during the vulnerability window (months 4–14); step down to 4–6 months once a second source is live | Buffer bridges to qualification, not to an arbitrary 6 months |
| **3. Reduce cutoff probability** | Stealth buffer build (§5, P-2); early LTA with continuity-of-supply and 12-month termination notice; executive reset with parent; no premature volume threats | Lowers p during the window we cannot yet cover |
| **4. Residual-gap contingency** | Allocation triage (prioritize contractual-penalty and high-margin lines); finished-goods pre-build; customer communication templates; vetted broker/spot protocol with quality screening; engineering workarounds (re-grading, alternate lots) | Converts an existential gap into a managed revenue loss |

**Stated plainly:** the gap cannot be fully closed before roughly month 12. Until then, survival rests on levers 2 and 3. This is the honest reason the buffer is large and the relationship track is genuine rather than cosmetic.

---

## 4. Option Assessment

| Option | Role | Timeline | Cost profile | Key limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Dual-sourcing** | Shortens the clock — the structural fix | 12–14 mo with tooling replication (18 without); +6 to ramp | $1–2M qualification; modest piece-price premium during ramp | Tacit know-how slows transfer; a 25–30% split already changes the negotiation — full parity is not the goal |
| **Strategic inventory** | Bridges the clock | Buildable in 2–3 quarters | Carrying ~15–25%/yr; peak 9–12-month buffer ≈ 15–20% of annual spend/yr at illustrative volumes | Obsolescence if redesign commits — mitigated by composition review at the redesign gate and a buy-back clause in the LTA |
| **Contractual protections** | Cheapest protection; diagnostic either way | 3–9 months to negotiate | Premium 1–3% of spend, or traded for volume | Paper doesn't ship parts — but a refusal to sign is free intelligence |
| **Partial vertical integration** | Caps long-term dependency; credible leverage | 18–30 months | $5–10M capex pilot line + $1–2M/yr opex | Know-how is tacit; honest scope is a captive 20–40% capability, not full make |
| **Product redesign** | Removes the need for the clock | Delays next generation | $3–8M engineering + market-window cost | Largest, least reversible spend — and the only one that *ends* the dependency tax. Develop to decision-ready; gate the commitment |
| **Tooling replication** *(cross-cutting enabler)* | Compresses dual-source, vertical, *and* redesign timelines simultaneously | 4–6 months | $1.5–3M one-time | None material — arguably the highest-leverage single action in the portfolio |

---

## 5. Recommended Portfolio

### Phase 0 (months 0–3) — quiet moves, cheap information

| # | Action | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|---|
| P-1 | **Tooling & IP audit**: ownership, condition, drawings, process documentation, change-of-control clauses in existing agreements | Legal + Engineering | Month 2 |
| P-2 | **Stealth buffer build (decided, not optional):** order within historical variability bands (±15%); route incremental volume through a third-party logistics partner holding stock off-site; build finished-goods buffer where shelf-life allows. **We accept the 3–5% channel margin as provocation insurance** — a visible hoard invites allocation and price action precisely during our exposed window | Procurement + 3PL | Start month 0; 3 mo coverage by month 3 |
| P-3 | **Executive outreach to the new parent** — senior-leader meeting framed as a strategic reset: stable volumes, joint cost-down, long-term partnership. Their response is diagnostic either way | CEO / BU President | Month 1–2 |
| P-4 | **Information hygiene:** forecasts bounded to 6-month rolling horizon; roadmap and generation timing withheld; single-channel communication | Program Owner | Month 1 |
| P-5 | Screen second-source candidates; down-select **two** | Engineering + Procurement | Month 3 |
| P-6 | Surveillance baseline (§7c): incoming inspection enhancement, SPC, tripwires | Quality | Month 3 |

### Phase 1 (months 3–9) — start the clock

| # | Action | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|---|
| T-1 | **Tooling branch (resolved, not just audited):** *If we own the tooling* — verify condition, secure drawings in escrow, establish relocation rights. *If the supplier owns it* — **fund replication at an independent toolmaker immediately**; this compresses every downstream timeline | Engineering | Order by month 4 |
| T-2 | Launch **parallel qualification** of both candidates, with replicated tooling and pre-agreed test plans | Engineering + Quality | Month 4; complete month 12–16 |
| T-3 | Negotiate the LTA (clause list and trades in §5a). **Signature deadline: month 9 — a missed deadline is itself a Tier 2 trigger** | CPO + Legal | Month 9 |
| T-4 | Commission vertical-integration feasibility (pilot line scope, licensing, selective hiring) | Engineering + Finance | Study by month 12 |
| T-5 | Develop redesign to **decision-ready** state (architecture, cost, schedule) without committing the generation | Engineering | Month 15 |

### Phase 2 (months 9–18) — gates
- Buffer at peak target (9–12 months); qualification past midpoint.
- **G2 (month 9):** LTA signed — or failure logged as Tier 2. Second candidate down-select to lead + backup.
- **G3 (month 12–15):** vertical pilot go/no-go. **G4 (month 15–18):** redesign commit vs. fold into following generation.

### Phase 3 (months 18–36) — independence, partial or full
- Lead second source ramped to 30–50% of volume; backup candidate kept warm.
- Captive capability live if G3 justified it.
- Next-generation architecture treats supplier dependency as a first-class design constraint.

### 5a. Contract workstream — clause list and trades

**Ask:** (1) index-linked pricing with cap/collar (±3–4%/yr) and a single annual negotiation window; (2) most-favored-customer pricing; (3) minimum supply term 3–5 years, termination notice ≥ 12 months, end-of-life notice ≥ 24 months with last-time-buy rights; (4) reserved capacity ≥ 120% of rolling forecast; (5) OTIF ≥ 95% with liquidated damages and expedite-at-supplier-cost; (6) change-of-control notification within 30 days, NDA reaffirmation binding the parent, termination right on any *further* change of control; (7) tooling ownership acknowledgment (or purchase option at net book value) with inspection and 60-day relocation rights; (8) escrow of process documentation with license to use for alternate-source qualification upon supply failure; (9) audit rights — quality, capacity, financials, information security; (10) supplier buy-back of buffer stock rendered obsolete by redesign.

**Trade (face-saving, bounded):** 2–3 year volume commitment at 70–80% of demand (preserving the split option); term length; bounded forecast sharing; a joint cost-down program the supplier's new owner can present internally as a win.

---

## 6. Cost Logic — Parametric Model

**Expected annual dependency cost:** `E = S·r + p·(D·t) + V`

| Variable | Meaning | Illustrative value |
|---|---|---|
| S | Annual component spend | $20M |
| r | Annual price cadence above index | 8% → **$1.6M/yr** |
| p | Annual probability of ≥30-day disruption | 15% |
| D·t | Line-down cost/day × days | $250K × 30 → **$1.1M/yr expected** |
| V | Strategic cost of competitor visibility | Qualitative; treat as ≥ 0 |

**E ≈ $2.7M/yr before V.** Finance to populate actuals in Phase 0 — the model is falsifiable by design.

**Portfolio cost (illustrative):**

| Item | One-time | Recurring |
|---|---|---|
| Tooling replication | $1.5–3M | — |
| Parallel qualification (2 candidates) | $1–2M | $0.2–0.4M/yr ramp premium |
| Buffer (peak 9–12 mo ≈ $15–20M inventory) | — | $3–4M/yr carrying at peak, stepping to ~$1.3M/yr at 4–6 mo. **Recoverable working capital, not sunk cost** |
| LTA premium | — | 0–3% of S (traded for volume if possible) |
| Vertical pilot *(gated)* | $5–10M | $1–2M/yr |
| Redesign to decision-ready *(gated for commitment)* | $0.5–1M | $3–8M only if committed |

**Envelope:** Year 1 ≈ **$6–9M**; Years 2–3 ≈ **$2–4M/yr** steady state; G3/G4 decisions carry separate business cases.
**Payback:** tooling + qualification (~$3–5M) against a recurring tax of ~$2.7M/yr → **~2-year payback on price defense alone**; at even p = 5%, disruption avoidance is additive. A single 30-day line-down repays a full year of peak buffer carrying cost.

---

## 7. Escalation Triggers — Defined, Valued, Time-Conditional

*Values are defaults; calibrate to the 12-month baseline in Phase 0. Pre-committed here so they cannot be renegotiated under pressure.*

### 7a. Trigger definitions

| Tier | Trigger (any one fires the tier) |
|---|---|
| **1 — Monitor** | Baseline: OTIF ≥ 92%; pricing within index + 3 pts; lead time stable; no surveillance flags |
| **2 — Contain** | OTIF < 92% for two consecutive quarters, or any quarter < 85% • Cumulative price movement > 8% above index in trailing 12 months, or any unilateral increase outside the annual window • Lead time +25% sustained 60 days • LTA unsigned at month 9 • MOQ increase > 50% or volume-lock demand without reciprocal capacity commitment • Demand for roadmap visibility beyond 6-month rolling forecast • Withdrawal of application engineering support • PPM > 1.5× baseline for two consecutive months, or any unreported process/site change |
| **3 — Independence** | Confirmed information leakage (tripwire fired, or competitor announcement matching non-public roadmap within 2 quarters) • Allocation or preferential treatment of the parent/competitor during shortage • Refusal to release tooling we own
